```{r knitr_setup, include=FALSE}
# === GLOBAL KNITR OPTIONS ===

#                    exploratory appendix that a reviewer should be able to audit
#                    line by line, so nothing is hidden.
# warning/message  : suppressed in the OUTPUT only (they still fire in the
#                    console). psych::alpha, psych::fa, and psych::omega are all
```

# Overview

This document is the **supplementary / exploratory** analysis for the Retribution
study. It sits downstream of `01_main_analysis.Rmd`, which owns cleaning, the
pre-registered exclusions, scoring, reliability, and the confirmatory tests
H1–H21, and which writes the scored dataset this document consumes,
`data/cleaned/retribution_scored.csv`. The language hypotheses E3–E7 live in
`02_nlp_integration.Rmd`; nothing in this file duplicates them.

Everything here is **exploratory**. Pre-registration Section 6.6 states that these
analyses "are exploratory and are not corrected as a confirmatory family." No
false-discovery-rate correction is applied across the tests in this document.
Where a prediction names a direction (E1, E2) we report the one-sided p-value in
the predicted direction alongside the two-sided p-value, per Section 6.8.

## Why nothing in this document is FDR-corrected (Section 6.6)

This is the single most important thing to understand before reading any p-value
below, so it is stated once here and repeated at each phase.

The pre-registration nominates exactly two multiplicity families, and this
document belongs to neither:

  1. **H1** — the set of correlations between punitiveness and each correlate.
     Sections 6.1 and 6.3 control the false discovery rate with
     Benjamini–Hochberg *across that set*, and report adjusted and unadjusted
     p-values side by side. That correction lives in `01_main_analysis.Rmd`.
  2. **E3–E7** — the language hypotheses. Section 6.7: "E3 through E7 form one
     exploratory family; we control the false discovery rate within it." That
     correction lives in `02_nlp_integration.Rmd`, not here.

Everything in *this* file — E1, E2, the factor structure, the sentence change,
the moderators, the measure agreement, the response-quality report — is covered
by the closing sentence of Section 6.6: "These analyses are exploratory and are
not corrected as a confirmatory family."

Three reasons make that the right call rather than a loophole, and a reader
should hold all three:

  - **A family is a pre-specified set, not a page of a document.** BH-FDR
    controls the expected proportion of false discoveries *within a declared
    family*. The tests below do not form one: E1 is five personality outcomes,
    E2 is a single Steiger comparison of two correlations, the EFA is a
    descriptive decomposition with no null hypothesis at all, the moderator
    models are eight interaction terms, and the agreement analysis is a
    reliability report. Pooling them into one BH sweep would be an
    *un*-preregistered analytic choice — it would invent a family the plan never
    declared, and the number it produced would be a researcher degree of freedom
    rather than a control.
  - **The inferential weight was never placed here.** Section 2.4 labels E1 and
    E2 "exploratory predictions"; Section 6.6 keeps them out of the confirmatory
    machinery. Nothing below is offered as a confirmed effect, so there is no
    confirmatory error rate to protect. The correct reading of a small p-value
    in this document is "worth a confirmatory test in a future study," not
    "established."
  - **Correcting would be misleading in the other direction.** Applying BH here
    would dress these analyses in confirmatory clothing and invite exactly the
    over-reading the exploratory label is meant to prevent. It would also imply
    the family had been fixed in advance, which it was not.

**Practical consequence for the reader.** Every p-value printed below is
unadjusted. Treat them descriptively, alongside the effect size and confidence
interval that Section 6.8 requires for every test. A nominally significant
result here is a lead, not a finding.

One deliberate exception to the "no correction" rule is worth naming: the
alpha = .05 threshold and the one-sided/two-sided rule from Section 6.8 are
still applied, because those are *inference conventions*, not multiplicity
adjustments. Directional predictions (E1's five signed predictions, E2's
"more strongly than") are tested one-sided in the predicted direction; the
report-only analyses, which name no direction, stay two-sided.

## Pre-registered hypotheses

  - **E1** — Retributivists score higher than non-retributivists on Right-Wing
    Authoritarianism, Social Dominance Orientation, violence proneness, and
    racial resentment, and **lower** on cognitive reflection (CRT). Tested "with
    the same methods" as the confirmatory group contrasts (Section 6.5): Welch
    t-tests with Cohen's d, run under **each** retributivist definition, plus a
    continuous regression so the result does not depend on a split.
  - **E2** — Hostile solidarity (social exclusion of offenders,
    `exclusion_1`–`exclusion_3`) relates to punitiveness more strongly than
    Durkheimian solidarity (`Solidarity_2`, `Solidarity_3`). Compared with
    **Steiger's test** for dependent, overlapping correlations.
    Per Section 5.3, `Solidarity_1` ("Removing criminals from society helps
    society cleanse itself") is **dropped** from the Durkheimian reading because
    it is exclusionary rather than Durkheimian; a sensitivity check that puts it
    back is reported alongside.

Section 6.6 names three further report-only analyses, and Sections 5.3 and 6.2
add two more. Together they make up the rest of this document:

  - the **factor structure of the correlates** (EFA + scree, extending H3);
  - the **change from the first to the second sentence** as a function of
    retributivism, including the pre-registered regression-adjusted robustness
    version in which the second sentence is residualized on the first
    (Sections 5.3, 5.11);
  - **political orientation** and the **prosecution–defense leaning** as
    moderators (Section 5.13);
  - the **agreement among the four retributivist definitions** required by
    Section 5.3 ("we report their pairwise agreement and the overlap among the
    groups they define"): the ranking, the relative retribution subscale, the
    sentencing ratio, and the exploratory semantic measure;
  - the **completion-time and long-string response-quality report** that
    Section 6.2 asks for as a diagnostic that does **not** remove anyone from the
    confirmatory analyses.

## Phases

  1. **Phase 0** — Setup, paths, packages, helper functions
  2. **Phase 1** — Load the scored data (or rebuild it), derive supplementary variables
  3. **Phase 2** — E1: personality and cognitive reflection between groups
  4. **Phase 3** — E2: hostile vs. Durkheimian solidarity (Steiger's test)
  5. **Phase 4** — Factor structure of the correlates (EFA + scree)
  6. **Phase 5** — Change from the first to the second sentence
  7. **Phase 6** — Political orientation and prosecution–defense leaning as moderators
  8. **Phase 7** — Agreement and overlap among the four retributivist definitions
  9. **Phase 8** — Response-quality report (completion time, long strings)
  10. **Phase 9** — Save all output files

## Data note

The analysis file is the Qualtrics **Values** export (numeric, 1–7). The
companion **Labels** export is a codebook only — it mixes anchor text with bare
numbers at the middle scale points, so it cannot be used for numeric work.

The export carries three header rows (variable names, question text, ImportId
JSON), so it is read by taking the names from row 1 and then skipping three rows.
The sentencing block is **vignette-split**: `Sentence1_V1_1` / `_V2_1` / `_V3_1`,
and likewise for `Sentence2` and the two open-ends. These are coalesced using the
embedded `Vignette` field (1/2/3). Slider exports carry a trailing `_1`
(`CRT_1_1`, `age_1`, `Sentence1_V1_1`). The ranking explanation exports as
`Priorit_Explain`; the pre-registration calls it `Q333`.

Two measurement rules matter throughout and are enforced here:

  - `severity_1` is reverse-keyed **only** inside the just-deserts proportionality
    component, never for the standalone H4/H5 severity items.
  - `punitiveness` (the 8 self-report items) is used wherever the sentence
    appears on the other side of a test; `punitiveness_full` (which adds the
    within-vignette standardized sentence) is **never** used in that situation.
    Section 5.3 and 5.11 require this, and it binds most of Phase 5 and Phase 7
    of this document.

The analysis file is `Data/FullData_Values.csv`: 1,015 raw responses, N = 948
after the Section 6.2 exclusions, with the three vignettes at 315 / 317 / 316.
Collection stopped at the target under the Section 4.4 stopping rule, so
everything below runs on the final sample. `Data/` also holds an interim partial
export (`Pilot_300_*`); always read the full file.

## Output organization

  - `output/tables/` — CSV tables (contrasts, correlations, EFA loadings, agreement)
  - `output/figures/` — PNG figures (scree plot, sentence change, response quality)
  - `data/cleaned/` — the supplementary variables derived here, for downstream use

# PHASE 0: SETUP AND PACKAGE LOADING

```{r phase0_paths}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 0.1 — PATH CONFIGURATION
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: declares every input and output path used by the whole
# document, creates the three output directories if they do not exist, and
# prints a existence check so a failed knit reports WHICH file was missing
# rather than dying with an opaque read error 400 lines later.
#
# WRITES: nothing to disk except three (possibly empty) directories.
# OBJECTS CREATED: SCORED_CSV, DATA_RAW, SEMANTIC_CSV, OUT_TABLES, OUT_FIGURES,
#                  OUT_DATA — all consumed by later phases.
# ===========================================================================

# === PATH CONFIGURATION ===
# All paths are relative to this .Rmd file's folder,
#   Retribution/Analysis/Retribution R/ .
# Knit from that folder (RStudio does this automatically).
#
# WHY RELATIVE PATHS: this pipeline lives in a shared Google Drive folder whose
# absolute prefix differs on every collaborator's machine. Relative paths make
# the document portable; the cost is that the working directory must be the
# .Rmd's own folder, which is what knitr does by default.

# Primary input: the scored file written by 01_main_analysis.Rmd.
# This is the intended path. 01 owns cleaning, exclusions, reverse coding, and
# the composites; this document should consume its output, not re-derive it.
SCORED_CSV <- file.path("data", "cleaned", "retribution_scored.csv")

# Fallback input: the raw Qualtrics VALUES export, two levels up.
# NOTE ON WHICH EXPORT: the VALUES export is numeric (1-7). The companion LABELS
# export writes anchor TEXT at the endpoints but bare NUMBERS at the middle
# scale points, so coercing it to numeric silently produces NAs at exactly the
# scale positions that matter most. Never point DATA_RAW at the Labels file.
# FullData_Values.csv is the complete collection: 1,015 raw responses, N = 948
# after the Section 6.2 exclusions. Data/ also holds an interim partial export
# (Pilot_300_*); always read the full file.
DATA_RAW <- file.path("..", "..", "Data", "FullData_Values.csv")

# Optional input: the dictionary-based facet scores from the NLP pipeline.
# Used only as a PROVISIONAL stand-in for the semantic measure (Phase 7).
# The word list is one of the two NON-MODEL safeguards named in Section 6.7, so
# it is a defensible placeholder, but it is NOT the validated LLM-ensemble
# semantic measure the pre-registration calls the fourth retributivist
# definition. Phase 1.4 labels it as provisional wherever it is used.
SEMANTIC_CSV <- file.path("..", "NLP", "outputs", "facet_dictionary_scores.csv")

# Output directories
# Kept separate so the knitted appendix, the machine-readable tables, and the
# derived variables can be shared or re-generated independently.
OUT_TABLES  <- file.path("output", "tables")   # CSV tables (contrasts, r's, EFA)
OUT_FIGURES <- file.path("output", "figures")  # PNG figures (scree, histograms)
OUT_DATA    <- file.path("data", "cleaned")    # derived supplementary variables

# recursive = TRUE creates intermediate folders; showWarnings = FALSE keeps the
# knit quiet when the directory already exists (the normal case on a re-knit).
for (dir_ in c(OUT_TABLES, OUT_FIGURES, OUT_DATA)) {
  dir.create(dir_, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
}

# normalizePath() is called only AFTER dir.create(), because it errors on a
# path that does not yet exist. Printing the absolute path here is the fastest
# way to diagnose a knit that silently wrote its output to the wrong folder.

cat("Output directories ready:\n")
cat("  Tables:  ", normalizePath(OUT_TABLES),  "\n")
cat("  Figures: ", normalizePath(OUT_FIGURES), "\n")
cat("  Cleaned: ", normalizePath(OUT_DATA),    "\n\n")
cat("Inputs:\n")
cat(sprintf("  scored CSV (from 01):  %-55s exists = %s\n",
            SCORED_CSV, file.exists(SCORED_CSV)))
cat(sprintf("  raw VALUES export:     %-55s exists = %s\n",
            DATA_RAW, file.exists(DATA_RAW)))
cat(sprintf("  NLP facet scores:      %-55s exists = %s\n",
            SEMANTIC_CSV, file.exists(SEMANTIC_CSV)))
```

```{r phase0_packages}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 0.2 — PACKAGE LOADING
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reports any missing package (rather than crashing at
# the first library() call), loads whatever IS installed, and records whether
# GPArotation is present, which decides the EFA rotation in Phase 4.
#
# WHY THE "REPORT, DON'T STOP" DESIGN: a collaborator opening this file for the
# first time gets one readable list of what to install, instead of fixing one
# missing package per failed knit.
# ===========================================================================

# === PACKAGE LOADING ===
# Each package's purpose is annotated for transparency.

required_packages <- c(
  "readr",        # Fast CSV reading with explicit header handling
  "dplyr",        # Data manipulation
  "tidyr",        # Reshaping for the figures
  "ggplot2",      # Figures
  "psych",        # Alpha/omega, EFA, parallel analysis, Cohen's kappa
  "cocor",        # Steiger's test for dependent, overlapping correlations
  "broom",        # tidy() for regression output
  "knitr"         # kable() tables in the knitted document
)

# Report-then-continue: name every missing package in one message rather than
# aborting the knit on the first one.
installed <- rownames(installed.packages())
missing_pkgs <- setdiff(required_packages, installed)
if (length(missing_pkgs)) {
  cat("Missing packages (install before knitting):",
      paste(missing_pkgs, collapse = ", "), "\n")
}

# Load only what is actually installed. character.only = TRUE is required
# because we are passing package names as strings, not as bare symbols.
# invisible() suppresses the list of attached-package vectors lapply returns.
invisible(lapply(intersect(required_packages, installed),
                 library, character.only = TRUE))

# GPArotation is needed for oblique EFA rotation; the EFA chunk falls back to
# an orthogonal rotation if it is absent.
# WHY THIS MATTERS SUBSTANTIVELY: oblimin (oblique) lets the extracted factors
# correlate, which is the theoretically right assumption here — H3 is precisely
# the claim that ONE punitiveness dimension runs through the correlates, so
# forcing the factors orthogonal (varimax) would assume the answer away. The
# varimax fallback keeps the document knittable but should be flagged in any
# write-up, because it changes the loadings.
# requireNamespace() tests availability WITHOUT attaching the package: psych
# calls GPArotation internally, so it never needs to be on the search path.
HAS_GPA <- requireNamespace("GPArotation", quietly = TRUE)

# scipen = 999 pushes R hard away from scientific notation, so a p-value prints
# as 0.000000123 rather than 1.23e-07. format_p() handles the display rule
# ("< .001") for text; this option governs raw print()/kable() output.
options(scipen = 999)  # No scientific notation in printed output
# 4 significant digits is a display setting only -- it does not round any stored
# value, so no computed result changes.
options(digits = 4)

cat("\nPackages loaded. GPArotation available:", HAS_GPA, "\n")
```

```{r phase0_helpers}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 0.3 — HELPER FUNCTIONS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: defines every function reused below, plus the mutable
# `alpha_table` reliability log. Nothing here reads data or produces a result;
# the chunk's only printed output is the roll-call at the end.
#
# These are the same helpers the Dark Side / Punishment 2.1 pipeline uses, so a
# reader who knows that codebase can skip ahead, plus four contrast helpers
# specific to this document: welch_contrast(), run_contrasts(),
# steiger_overlap(), and balanced_split().
#
# EVERY function is defensive in the same way: it returns NULL or NA rather
# than raising, so that one absent column cannot abort the knit 800 lines
# later. The cost is that a silent NULL means "not estimable", and each call
# site below checks for it before displaying.
# ===========================================================================

# === HELPER FUNCTIONS ===

#' Format a p-value for display in prose written with cat()/sprintf().
#'
#' Returns a string that reads correctly after the word "p": "< .001" or
#' "= 0.037". Anything below .001 is reported as "< .001" rather than as a
#' string of zeros, which is the usual reporting convention and avoids implying
#' more precision than a p-value carries. Scalar-only by design: a vector of
#' p-values goes to sig_stars() or straight into a kable column instead.
format_p <- function(p) {
  if (length(p) != 1 || is.na(p)) return("NA")
  if (p < .001) return("< .001")
  sprintf("= %.3f", p)
}

#' Convert p-values to significance stars. Vectorized (case_when), so it can be
#' applied to a whole column of a results table.
#'
#' The thresholds are the conventional .001 / .01 / .05 ladder. The .05 rung is
#' the Section 6.8 alpha. NOTE that every star printed in this document marks an
#' UNADJUSTED p-value: Section 6.6 places these analyses outside both
#' multiplicity families, so a star here flags a lead worth a confirmatory test,
#' not a controlled discovery.
sig_stars <- function(p) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    is.na(p) ~ "",
    p < .001 ~ "***",
    p < .01  ~ "**",
    p < .05  ~ "*",
    TRUE     ~ ""
  )
}

# Reverse a 1..7 item so that a higher score means more of the named construct.
# The constant is 8 because it is (scale minimum + scale maximum) = 1 + 7; a
# 1-5 item would need 6 instead. Every attitude item in this study is on the
# seven-point agree-disagree scale of Section 5.1, so one constant covers all of
# them. Applying rev7() twice restores the original value, which is exactly the
# failure mode to watch for with Retribution_6 and Retribution_7 (see Phase 1.2).
rev7 <- function(x) 8 - x

# Reliability log, filled by compute_composite() through the `<<-` on each call.
# Declared here and RESET at the top of Phase 1.2, so a re-run of that chunk
# alone does not append a second copy of every row.
alpha_table <- data.frame()

#' Composite = row-mean of items, with Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega
#' logged into `alpha_table`.
#'
#' Arguments:
#'   data         data frame holding the items.
#'   items        character vector of item names; missing ones are dropped.
#'   name         label written into the reliability log.
#'   reverse_ok   passed to psych::alpha() as check.keys. Left FALSE almost
#'                everywhere here, because reverse coding is done explicitly
#'                upstream (the *_R columns) and letting alpha silently flip a
#'                key would hide a scoring error rather than surface it.
#'   print_output print a one-line alpha/omega summary as a side effect.
#' Returns: numeric vector of length nrow(data), the composite score.
#'
#' Reused by every composite built in Phase 1.2.
compute_composite <- function(data, items, name, reverse_ok = FALSE,
                              print_output = FALSE) {
  # Tolerate a caller naming items that are not in this particular export.
  items <- intersect(items, names(data))
  if (!length(items)) return(rep(NA_real_, nrow(data)))

  item_data    <- as.data.frame(data[, items, drop = FALSE])
  # Section 5.1: "computed for anyone who answered at least half of the items."
  # ceiling() makes the rule strict on odd k -- a 7-item scale needs 4 answers,
  # not 3.5 rounded down. Everything below the threshold becomes NA rather than
  # a mean of one or two items, which would be on a different scale in practice.
  min_answered <- ceiling(length(items) / 2)
  n_answered   <- rowSums(!is.na(item_data))
  comp         <- rowMeans(item_data, na.rm = TRUE)
  comp[n_answered < min_answered] <- NA_real_

  # Section 5.1 asks for BOTH alpha and omega on every composite. Two-item
  # composites still get an alpha (it is just the Spearman-Brown stepped-up
  # correlation there); single-item "composites" get neither, hence k >= 2.
  a <- o <- NA_real_
  if (length(items) >= 2) {
    # tryCatch keeps a Heywood case or a singular item matrix from aborting the
    # knit: the reliability cell reports NA and the composite itself still
    # computes, since the row-mean above does not depend on either estimate.
    a <- tryCatch(psych::alpha(item_data, check.keys = reverse_ok,
                               warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha,
                  error = function(e) NA_real_)
    # omega.tot is the total omega (all common variance), which is the
    # comparable figure to raw alpha. nfactors = 1 fits the single-factor model
    # these composites assume; plot = FALSE stops psych from opening a device
    # mid-knit.
    o <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
                    psych::omega(item_data, nfactors = 1,
                                 plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)),
                  error = function(e) NA_real_)
  }
  # `<<-` writes to the alpha_table in the enclosing (global) environment. The
  # item list is stored verbatim so the printed table carries its own
  # provenance -- a reader can see which columns, reversed or not, went in.
  alpha_table <<- rbind(
    alpha_table,
    data.frame(composite = name, k = length(items), alpha = a, omega = o,
               items = paste(items, collapse = ", "),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  )
  if (print_output) {
    cat(sprintf("  %-30s k=%d  alpha=%s  omega=%s\n", name, length(items),
                ifelse(is.na(a), "  -  ", sprintf("%.3f", a)),
                ifelse(is.na(o), "  -  ", sprintf("%.3f", o))))
  }
  comp
}

#' Correlation with 95% CI, p, and pairwise n.
#'
#' Arguments: x, y are column NAMES; data is the frame holding them.
#' Returns: a named numeric vector c(r, ci_lower, ci_upper, p, n).
#'
#' Section 6.8 requires an effect size and a confidence interval on every test,
#' so the CI travels with the coefficient rather than being reconstructed later.
#' Pearson throughout, per Section 6.1.
#'
#' `n` is the PAIRWISE complete-case count, and it is returned even in the
#' failure branch: when a correlation is not estimable, the reader still needs
#' to see whether that was because of two cases or two hundred.
#'
#' Reused by E2 (Phase 3), the sentence analyses (Phase 5), the moderators
#' (Phase 6), and the measure-agreement tables (Phase 7).
get_cor_ci <- function(x, y, data) {
  xv <- data[[x]]; yv <- data[[y]]
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(xv, yv)
  # Guard on two failure modes cor.test() would either error on or answer
  # nonsensically: too few pairs for a CI (n < 4 leaves no residual df once the
  # Fisher-z interval is formed), and a constant vector (sd == 0), which makes
  # the correlation undefined -- the sentencing ratio can be constant inside a
  # small subgroup, and the semantic placeholder is constant when absent.
  if (sum(ok) < 4 || stats::sd(xv[ok], na.rm = TRUE) == 0 ||
      stats::sd(yv[ok], na.rm = TRUE) == 0) {
    return(c(r = NA_real_, ci_lower = NA_real_, ci_upper = NA_real_,
             p = NA_real_, n = sum(ok)))
  }
  tst <- stats::cor.test(xv[ok], yv[ok])
  # unname() strips cor.test's "cor" label so the returned vector's own names
  # survive; without it the element would come back named "r.cor".
  c(r        = unname(tst$estimate),
    ci_lower = tst$conf.int[1],
    ci_upper = tst$conf.int[2],
    p        = tst$p.value,
    n        = sum(ok))
}

#' Format a correlation matrix as character cells with significance stars.
#'
#' Arguments: cor_matrix and p_matrix must share dimensions and dimnames.
#' Returns: a character matrix, diagonal blanked to "-".
#'
#' Used once, for the H1 correlate intercorrelations in Phase 4. That call
#' passes a matrix of ZEROS as p_matrix, which stars every off-diagonal cell:
#' the table is there to show the sign pattern H3 summarizes (the share of
#' positive intercorrelations), not to test 66 individual correlations, and
#' Section 6.6 places no multiplicity family around it.
format_cor_table <- function(cor_matrix, p_matrix, decimals = 2) {
  r_formatted <- round(cor_matrix, decimals)
  stars_vec   <- sig_stars(as.vector(p_matrix))
  # as.vector() unrolls column-major and matrix() re-rolls the same way, so the
  # r's and their stars stay aligned cell for cell.
  values_vec  <- paste0(format(as.vector(r_formatted), nsmall = decimals),
                        stars_vec)
  result <- matrix(values_vec, nrow = nrow(cor_matrix),
                   dimnames = dimnames(cor_matrix))
  # The diagonal is 1.00 by construction and carries no information; blanking it
  # keeps the eye on the off-diagonal pattern.
  diag(result) <- "-"
  result
}

#' Welch t-test + Cohen's d (high group minus low group) with a large-sample CI.
#'
#' Arguments:
#'   data       frame holding both columns.
#'   var        outcome column name (coerced to numeric).
#'   group      two-level grouping column; its factor LEVEL ORDER defines which
#'              side is "low" and which is "high".
#'   direction  the E1/E2-style predicted direction for the HIGH group:
#'              "greater" = high group scores higher, "less" = high group scores
#'              lower, "two.sided" = no directional prediction.
#'   label      human-readable name of the grouping, carried into the output so
#'              stacked tables stay readable.
#' Returns: a one-row data frame, or NULL when the contrast is not estimable.
#'
#' WHY WELCH RATHER THAN STUDENT: Section 6.5 fixes Welch t-tests for the group
#' contrasts. The retributivist groups are unequal in size (the ranking
#' definition splits roughly a third to two thirds) and there is no reason to
#' assume the two groups have equal variance on RWA, SDO, or the sentence
#' change. Student's t is badly behaved in exactly that combination -- unequal n
#' paired with unequal variance -- while Welch costs almost nothing when the
#' variances happen to match. stats::t.test() defaults to Welch, so no argument
#' is needed; the fractional `df` in the output is the Welch-Satterthwaite
#' correction and is the visible sign that it was used.
welch_contrast <- function(data, var, group, direction = "two.sided",
                           label = NA_character_) {
  if (!all(c(var, group) %in% names(data))) return(NULL)
  y <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[var]]))
  g <- data[[group]]
  ok <- !is.na(y) & !is.na(g)
  # droplevels() matters for grp_tert, which is built with the middle third set
  # to NA: without it the factor would still carry an empty level and nlevels()
  # would not equal 2.
  y <- y[ok]; g <- droplevels(factor(g[ok]))
  # Three or fewer per cell gives a variance estimate not worth reporting; a
  # constant outcome gives no test at all. Both return NULL, and run_contrasts()
  # simply omits the row.
  if (nlevels(g) != 2 || any(table(g) < 3)) return(NULL)
  if (stats::sd(y) == 0) return(NULL)

  lv  <- levels(g)
  y1  <- y[g == lv[1]]; y2 <- y[g == lv[2]]
  n1  <- length(y1);    n2 <- length(y2)
  m1  <- mean(y1);      m2 <- mean(y2)
  # y2 first, y1 second, so t and d both read HIGH MINUS LOW. Every grouping
  # factor built in Phase 1.3 is constructed with the low level first precisely
  # so this orientation holds; reversing a levels= argument there would silently
  # flip the sign of every d in the document.
  tt  <- stats::t.test(y2, y1)   # high minus low

  # Cohen's d uses the POOLED SD, not Welch's separate-variance denominator.
  # The pooled standardizer is what "Cohen's d" conventionally means and what
  # keeps d comparable across the four retributivist definitions, which differ
  # in how they split the sample. The test statistic stays Welch; only the
  # effect size is pooled.
  s_p  <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * stats::var(y1) + (n2 - 1) * stats::var(y2)) /
                 (n1 + n2 - 2))
  dval <- if (is.finite(s_p) && s_p > 0) (m2 - m1) / s_p else NA_real_
  # Hedges & Olkin's large-sample standard error for d: the first term is
  # sampling error in the mean difference, the second the error in estimating
  # the standardizer. It is the usual normal-approximation SE and is adequate
  # at these cell sizes (hundreds), which is why the CI below uses 1.96 rather
  # than a t quantile.
  se_d <- if (is.na(dval)) NA_real_ else
    sqrt((n1 + n2) / (n1 * n2) + dval^2 / (2 * (n1 + n2)))

  # Section 6.8: "Predictions that name a direction are tested one-sided in that
  # direction; the rest are two-sided." Both p-values are reported side by side
  # so a reader can apply either convention.
  #
  # The halving rule: when the observed t falls on the predicted side, the
  # one-sided p is half the two-sided p; when it falls on the wrong side, the
  # one-sided p is 1 - p_two/2, which is above .5 and correctly records that a
  # directional prediction cannot be supported by a result in the opposite
  # direction. Anything other than "greater"/"less" falls through to p_two.
  p_two <- tt$p.value
  p_dir <- switch(
    direction,
    greater = if (unname(tt$statistic) > 0) p_two / 2 else 1 - p_two / 2,
    less    = if (unname(tt$statistic) < 0) p_two / 2 else 1 - p_two / 2,
    p_two
  )

  # One row per contrast. Both level LABELS are carried alongside the means so a
  # stacked table cannot be misread about which side is which; `direction`
  # records the prediction that produced p_directional, so a reader never has to
  # guess whether a one-sided p was appropriate for that row.
  # The CI on d is the normal-approximation d +/- 1.96 * SE (95%).
  data.frame(
    grouping  = ifelse(is.na(label), group, label),
    variable  = var,
    level_low = lv[1], level_high = lv[2],
    n_low = n1, n_high = n2,
    M_low = m1, M_high = m2,
    t = unname(tt$statistic), df = unname(tt$parameter),
    p_two_sided = p_two,
    direction = direction,
    p_directional = p_dir,
    d = dval,
    d_lo = dval - 1.96 * se_d,
    d_hi = dval + 1.96 * se_d,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

#' Run welch_contrast() over a set of variables for one grouping variable.
#'
#' Arguments:
#'   vars        outcome column names.
#'   group       one grouping column.
#'   directions  optional NAMED list mapping outcome -> "greater"/"less".
#'               Outcomes absent from the list default to "two.sided", which is
#'               the Section 6.8 rule: only a prediction that names a direction
#'               earns a one-sided test. Passing NULL (as the report-only
#'               analyses in Phases 5 and 6 do) makes every row two-sided.
#' Returns: a stacked data frame, or NULL if no contrast was estimable.
#'
#' This is the workhorse behind E1 (each of the four definitions), the sentence
#' change, the residualized sentence, and the moderator descriptives.
run_contrasts <- function(data, vars, group, directions = NULL,
                          label = NA_character_) {
  out <- lapply(vars, function(v) {
    dir_v <- if (!is.null(directions) && v %in% names(directions))
      directions[[v]] else "two.sided"
    welch_contrast(data, v, group, direction = dir_v, label = label)
  })
  # Drop the NULLs welch_contrast() returns for non-estimable contrasts before
  # rbind(), which would otherwise silently discard them anyway but leaves a
  # zero-row frame that show_table() would render as an empty table.
  out <- out[!vapply(out, is.null, logical(1))]
  if (!length(out)) return(NULL)
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

#' Steiger's test for two dependent, OVERLAPPING correlations that share
#' variable `j`: r(j,k) vs r(j,h).
#'
#' Arguments: j is the SHARED variable; k and h are the two competitors;
#'   alternative is "greater" when the prediction is r(j,k) > r(j,h).
#' Returns: list(table = one-row data frame, cocor = the cocor object), or NULL.
#'
#' WHY STEIGER: E2 asks whether punitiveness correlates MORE STRONGLY with
#' hostile solidarity than with Durkheimian solidarity. Both correlations are
#' measured on the same participants and both contain punitiveness, so they are
#' dependent and overlapping. Comparing them by eye, or by whether one clears
#' .05 and the other does not, ignores r(k,h) -- the correlation between the two
#' competitors -- which drives how much sampling error the two coefficients
#' share. Steiger's (1980) modified z takes r(k,h) into account explicitly, and
#' it is what Sections 6.3, 6.4, and 6.6 specify for H2, H10, and E2 alike.
#'
#' Reused for E2 itself and for both E2 specification checks in Phase 3.
steiger_overlap <- function(data, j, k, h, alternative = "two.sided") {
  if (!all(c(j, k, h) %in% names(data))) return(NULL)
  # LISTWISE, not pairwise: Steiger's z assumes one n and one covariance
  # structure across all three coefficients, so all three r's must come from the
  # same set of rows. Computing them pairwise would put three different n's into
  # a formula that takes one.
  cc <- stats::complete.cases(data[[j]], data[[k]], data[[h]])
  n  <- sum(cc)
  if (n < 10) return(NULL)
  r_jk <- stats::cor(data[[j]][cc], data[[k]][cc])
  r_jh <- stats::cor(data[[j]][cc], data[[h]][cc])
  # The correlation BETWEEN the two competitors. This is the term that makes the
  # test a dependent-samples test rather than two independent comparisons.
  r_kh <- stats::cor(data[[k]][cc], data[[h]][cc])

  # test = "steiger1980" pins the estimator: cocor offers several overlapping
  # tests (Pearson-Filon, Hotelling, Dunn-Clark, Meng), and naming one keeps the
  # reported z reproducible instead of depending on a package default.
  res <- tryCatch(
    cocor::cocor.dep.groups.overlap(
      r.jk = r_jk, r.jh = r_jh, r.kh = r_kh, n = n,
      alternative = alternative, test = "steiger1980"),
    error = function(e) NULL)

  # cocor returns an S4 object, so the statistic and p come out through the @
  # slot rather than $. If cocor failed, the table still prints the three r's
  # and their difference with z and p as NA.
  z <- p <- NA_real_
  if (!is.null(res)) {
    z <- unname(res@steiger1980$statistic)
    p <- unname(res@steiger1980$p.value)
  }
  list(
    table = data.frame(
      shared = j, comparison_1 = k, comparison_2 = h,
      r_1 = r_jk, r_2 = r_jh, r_between = r_kh,
      diff = r_jk - r_jh, n = n,
      steiger_z = z, p = p, alternative = alternative,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
    cocor = res
  )
}

#' Percent formatter for report text. Takes a PROPORTION (0-1) and returns a
#' string such as "34.2%", so call sites pass mean(flag) rather than 100*mean().
pct <- function(x, digits = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f%%"), 100 * x)

#' Print a data frame as a knitr table with sensible rounding.
#'
#' NOTE ON PLACEMENT: knitr prints the value of every *top-level* expression in
#' a chunk, so show_table() must be called at the top level, never buried inside
#' an if/else block where its value would be discarded. Every chunk below
#' follows that rule: results are computed under a guard, then displayed at the
#' top level. NULL and empty inputs are handled here.
show_table <- function(df, caption = NULL, digits = 3) {
  if (is.null(df) || !nrow(df)) {
    cat("(no rows to display)\n"); return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  # row.names = FALSE suppresses kable's 1..n gutter, which carries no meaning
  # for these stacked result tables and only invites a reader to cite a row
  # number that shifts whenever a contrast becomes non-estimable.
  knitr::kable(df, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE, caption = caption)
}

#' Select columns from a possibly-NULL data frame without erroring.
#'
#' Arguments: df may be NULL or zero-row; cols is a wish list.
#' Returns: df restricted to whichever of `cols` exist, or NULL.
#'
#' Used to display a readable subset of welch_contrast()'s wide output: the full
#' object keeps level_low/level_high/direction for the saved CSV, while the
#' printed table shows only what a reader needs on the page. intersect() rather
#' than a plain `[` means a table that lost a column (for example `df` when a
#' contrast was not estimable) still prints instead of raising.
pick_cols <- function(df, cols) {
  if (is.null(df) || !nrow(df)) return(NULL)
  df[, intersect(cols, names(df)), drop = FALSE]
}

#' Median split that is aware of ties.
#'
#' Arguments: x, a numeric vector.
#' Returns: list(split = 0/1 integer vector, rule = the comparison used,
#'   cut = the median itself).
#'
#' The sentencing ratio has a large point mass at exactly 1.0 (participants who
#' did not reduce the sentence at all), so a strict `x > median` split throws
#' almost everyone into one cell. This chooses whichever of `>` or `>=` gives
#' the more even split and reports which rule it used.
#'
#' Reporting `rule` is the point: the split is a data-dependent choice, and the
#' printed rule tells a reader exactly which participants ended up on which
#' side. On the ratio, ">= median" separates those who kept the whole sentence
#' from those who cut it, which is the substantive contrast Section 5.11
#' describes ("a higher ratio, meaning a smaller reduction"). Applied to the
#' relative retribution subscale and to the semantic placeholder as well, so all
#' three continuous definitions are dichotomized the same way.
balanced_split <- function(x) {
  m <- stats::median(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  strict <- as.integer(x >  m)
  loose  <- as.integer(x >= m)
  # Evenness = the size of the SMALLER cell as a proportion; it peaks at 0.5 for
  # a perfect split and falls to 0 when everyone lands on one side. Maximizing
  # it is what keeps the Welch contrast estimable and reasonably powered.
  evenness <- function(v) { p <- mean(v, na.rm = TRUE); min(p, 1 - p) }
  # isTRUE() guards the NA case: if x is entirely missing both comparisons are
  # NA, and the strict rule is returned rather than the condition erroring.
  if (isTRUE(evenness(loose) > evenness(strict)))
    list(split = loose,  rule = ">= median", cut = m)
  else
    list(split = strict, rule = "> median",  cut = m)
}

cat("Helper functions loaded:\n")
cat("  format_p()          — p-value formatting\n")
cat("  sig_stars()         — p -> stars\n")
cat("  compute_composite() — composite + alpha/omega, logged to alpha_table\n")
cat("  get_cor_ci()        — correlation with 95% CI\n")
cat("  format_cor_table()  — formatted correlation matrix\n")
cat("  welch_contrast()    — Welch t + Cohen's d with directional p\n")
cat("  run_contrasts()     — welch_contrast() over a variable set\n")
cat("  steiger_overlap()   — Steiger's test, dependent overlapping r's\n")
cat("  balanced_split()    — tie-aware median split\n")
cat("  show_table()        — kable wrapper tolerant of NULL/empty input\n")
```

# PHASE 1: DATA LOADING AND SUPPLEMENTARY VARIABLES

## 1.1 Load the scored dataset

The scored file from `01_main_analysis.Rmd` is the intended input. If it has not
been produced yet, this chunk falls back to the raw Values export and reproduces
the Section 6.2 exclusion funnel, so the document knits either way.

```{r phase1_load}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 1.1 — LOAD THE ANALYSIS DATA
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reads the scored file 01_main_analysis.Rmd writes; if
# that file is absent, falls back to the raw Qualtrics VALUES export and
# reproduces the Section 6.2 exclusion funnel so the document still knits.
# Either way it finishes by forcing every scale column to numeric.
#
# OBJECTS CREATED: `d` (the analysis frame used by every later phase),
#                  DATA_SOURCE (a provenance string printed in Phase 9),
#                  exclusion_funnel (NULL unless the fallback ran).
# PRODUCES: the row/column count and the funnel table in the knitted output.
#
# ON THE FUNNEL: 1,015 raw responses -> Finished == 1 -> Progress == 100 ->
# AttnCheck1 -> AttnCheck2 leaves N = 948, with the three vignettes at
# 315 / 317 / 316. Section 6.2 makes failing EITHER attention check sufficient,
# "since both are easy for an attentive respondent."
# ===========================================================================

# --- Column groups that must be numeric regardless of the input file ---
# Qualtrics writes every cell as text, and readr's type guessing sees a column
# of "1".."7" and infers numeric only when nothing else appears in the first
# `guess_max` rows. Listing the scale columns explicitly and coercing them below
# removes that dependence on row order. Open-ended text columns are deliberately
# ABSENT from this list so they stay character.
num_cols_spec <- c(
  paste0("Retribution_", 1:7), paste0("Deterrence_", 1:3),
  paste0("Incapacitation_", 1:2), paste0("Rehabilitation_", 1:2),
  paste0("Solidarity_", 1:3), paste0("Prioritization_", 1:4),
  "punishmore_1", "punishmore_2", "parsimony_1", "parsimony_2",
  "threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2", "LWOP", "deathpenalty", "AttnCheck1",
  paste0("revenge_", 1:4), "proportionality", "severity_1", "severity_2",
  paste0("exclusion_", 1:3), paste0("essential_", 1:4),
  paste0("Society_", 1:3), paste0("choice_", 1:2), "AttnCheck2",
  paste0("dueprocess_", 1:3), paste0("uncertain_", 1:4),
  paste0("rates_", 1:2), paste0("fear_", 1:3),
  paste0("hate_", 1:3), paste0("anger_", 1:2),
  paste0("degrad_", 1:3), paste0("suffer_", 1:2), paste0("prisonvi_", 1:2),
  paste0("harsh_", 1:3), paste0("rwa_", 1:5), paste0("sdo_", 1:8),
  paste0("vprone_", 1:4), paste0("Raceresent_", 1:4),
  # The CRT items are SLIDERS, and Qualtrics appends a trailing _1 to every
  # slider export, so the columns are CRT_1_1 / CRT_2_1 / CRT_3_1 rather than
  # CRT_1 / CRT_2 / CRT_3. Same story for age_1 and the sentence sliders.
  "CRT_1_1", "CRT_2_1", "CRT_3_1",
  # The sentencing block is VIGNETTE-SPLIT: each participant sees one of three
  # vignettes and answers the matching column, so six sentence columns exist and
  # each is populated for roughly a third of the sample. Phase 1.2 coalesces
  # them through the embedded Vignette field. Both the split columns and the
  # coalesced names are listed, because either may be present depending on
  # whether this document read 01's output or the raw export.
  "Sentence1_V1_1", "Sentence2_V1_1", "Sentence1_V2_1", "Sentence2_V2_1",
  "Sentence1_V3_1", "Sentence2_V3_1",
  "Sentence1", "Sentence2",
  "Shark_1", "Shark_2", "Shark_3", "age_1", "age", "gender", "race",
  # "lib/conserv" carries a slash in the Qualtrics tag itself, so it always
  # needs backtick or bracket access in R; Phase 6 copies it to `libcons`.
  "education", "lib/conserv", "PoliticalID", "leanPros_1", "leanPros_2",
  "Vignette", "Progress", "Finished", "Duration (in seconds)"
)

#' Read a Qualtrics VALUES export that carries three header rows.
#'
#' Row 1 = variable names, row 2 = the full question text, row 3 = the ImportId
#' JSON. Reading naively would make row 2 the first data row and coerce every
#' column to character. The two-pass approach takes the names from row 1 with
#' n_max = 0, then re-reads with skip = 3 and those names supplied.
#' guess_max = 10000 exceeds the 1,015 rows in the file, so readr's type guess
#' sees the whole column rather than its first 1,000 rows.
read_qualtrics_values <- function(path) {
  # THREE header rows: (1) variable names, (2) question text, (3) ImportId JSON.
  nm <- names(readr::read_csv(path, n_max = 0, show_col_types = FALSE))
  readr::read_csv(path, skip = 3, col_names = nm,
                  show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 10000)
}

# Provenance, printed at the end of this chunk and again in the Phase 9 summary,
# so a knitted copy always states which input it was built from.
DATA_SOURCE <- NA_character_
exclusion_funnel <- NULL

# PREFERRED PATH: 01 has already cleaned, excluded, reverse-coded, and scored.
if (file.exists(SCORED_CSV)) {

  d <- readr::read_csv(SCORED_CSV, show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 10000)
  # as.data.frame() drops the tibble class. Base-R `[` subsetting is used
  # throughout this document, and a tibble's `[` keeps returning a tibble where
  # a vector is wanted; the plain frame keeps that behaviour predictable.
  d <- as.data.frame(d)
  DATA_SOURCE <- "scored CSV from 01_clean_and_score"
  cat(sprintf("Loaded scored data: %d rows x %d columns\n  from %s\n",
              nrow(d), ncol(d), SCORED_CSV))

# FALLBACK PATH: no scored file, so rebuild from the raw export.
} else if (file.exists(DATA_RAW)) {

  raw <- as.data.frame(read_qualtrics_values(DATA_RAW))
  DATA_SOURCE <- "raw Qualtrics VALUES export (01 output not found)"
  cat(sprintf("01 output not found. Loaded RAW data: %d rows x %d columns\n  from %s\n",
              nrow(raw), ncol(raw), DATA_RAW))

  # suppressWarnings() absorbs the expected "NAs introduced by coercion" on the
  # handful of cells Qualtrics leaves as an empty string.
  nc <- intersect(num_cols_spec, names(raw))
  raw[nc] <- lapply(raw[nc], function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)))

  # Pre-registered exclusions (Section 6.2). Failing EITHER check is enough.
  # AttnCheck1 correct = 9 ("strongly agree"); AttnCheck2 correct = 4 ("15").
  #
  # BOTH constants are CHOICE POSITIONS, not the values a reader would guess:
  #   AttnCheck1 is the instructed-response item ("please select the strongly
  #   agree option") and its choices are sparsely coded 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 with
  #   9 = "Strongly agree" -- so it is NOT on the 1-7 scale the neighbouring
  #   punitiveness items use, and 7 would be the wrong test.
  #   AttnCheck2 asks "What is 8+7?" with choices 12, 16, 17, 15, 14, 13, 18;
  #   the correct answer 15 sits in POSITION 4, so the export carries 4, not 15.
  # The !is.na() half of each filter matters because a missing value would
  # otherwise propagate NA into the subscript and inject blank rows.
  #
  # Order is the reported order, and each step's surviving n is recorded so the
  # funnel can be printed. Progress == 100 is applied alongside Finished == 1;
  # in this export the two agree, so that step removes no one.
  fn <- c(loaded = nrow(raw))
  d  <- raw
  d  <- d[!is.na(d$Finished)   & d$Finished   == 1,   ]; fn["finished"]    <- nrow(d)
  d  <- d[!is.na(d$Progress)   & d$Progress   == 100,  ]; fn["progress100"] <- nrow(d)
  d  <- d[!is.na(d$AttnCheck1) & d$AttnCheck1 == 9,    ]; fn["attn_check_1"]<- nrow(d)
  d  <- d[!is.na(d$AttnCheck2) & d$AttnCheck2 == 4,    ]; fn["attn_check_2"]<- nrow(d)
  exclusion_funnel <- data.frame(step = names(fn), n = as.integer(fn),
                                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat("\nExclusion funnel (reproduced here because 01's output was absent):\n")
  print(exclusion_funnel, row.names = FALSE)

# No usable input at all: stop loudly rather than knit an empty document.
} else {
  stop("Neither the scored CSV nor the raw VALUES export could be found.")
}

# Coerce whatever numeric columns are present, whichever source we came from.
# Repeated deliberately: 01's scored CSV round-trips through text on write, so a
# column that is all-integer there can still come back as character.
nc <- intersect(num_cols_spec, names(d))
d[nc] <- lapply(d[nc], function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)))

cat(sprintf("\nData source: %s\nAnalysis N = %d\n", DATA_SOURCE, nrow(d)))
```

## 1.2 Rebuild the scored variables

The composites, reverse-coded items, and retributivist measures are recomputed
here from the item columns. This is deliberately idempotent: if `01` already put
them in the file they are reproduced identically, and if this document is run
against a raw export it still has everything it needs. Reliabilities are logged
so the supplementary tables carry their own provenance.

```{r phase1_derive}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 1.2 — REBUILD THE SCORED VARIABLES
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: coalesces the vignette-split columns, applies the
# reverse coding, standardizes the first sentence within vignette, and builds
# every composite this document needs, logging alpha and omega for each.
#
# WHY IT IS IDEMPOTENT: every derivation is guarded by a `!"name" %in% names(d)`
# test or recomputes to the same value, so running against 01's scored file
# reproduces what is already there and running against a raw export fills it in.
# Nothing here overwrites a column 01 owns with a different definition.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: Sections 5.1 - 5.12 (scoring conventions and composites).
# PRODUCES: the composite columns on `d`, and the printed reliability table.
# ===========================================================================

# Small predicate used as a guard before any multi-column derivation.
has_col <- function(v) all(v %in% names(d))

# --- Coalesce the vignette-split sentence columns (if not already done) ------
#' Collapse a set of _V1/_V2/_V3 columns into one, using the embedded Vignette
#' field to decide which source each participant's value comes from.
#'
#' Arguments: df, the frame; stem, the column stem ("Sentence1"); slider, TRUE
#'   when the export carries the trailing _1 that Qualtrics adds to sliders.
#' Returns: a vector of length nrow(df) with one value per participant.
#'
#' Each participant saw exactly ONE of the three vignettes (Section 3.2, random
#' assignment; the realized balance is 315 / 317 / 316), so the three source
#' columns are mutually exclusive and the coalesced column is complete. Reading
#' any single _V column instead would silently analyse a third of the sample.
pick_vig <- function(df, stem, slider = FALSE) {
  out <- rep(NA, nrow(df))
  for (v in 1:3) {
    # Sliders export as Sentence1_V1_1; free text exports as
    # Sentence_OpenEnd1_V1 with no suffix. Hence the `slider` switch.
    src <- paste0(stem, "_V", v, if (slider) "_1" else "")
    if (!src %in% names(df)) next
    # Assign only into the rows assigned to vignette v, so the three passes
    # write to disjoint slices and never overwrite each other.
    sel <- !is.na(df$Vignette) & df$Vignette == v
    out[sel] <- df[[src]][sel]
  }
  out
}
# Sentence1/Sentence2 are the 0-50 year sliders (50 = life, Section 5.11).
# as.numeric() because pick_vig() starts from a logical NA vector, so the
# result's type is only settled by what gets written into it.
if (!"Sentence1" %in% names(d) && "Sentence1_V1_1" %in% names(d))
  d$Sentence1 <- as.numeric(pick_vig(d, "Sentence1", slider = TRUE))
if (!"Sentence2" %in% names(d) && "Sentence2_V1_1" %in% names(d))
  d$Sentence2 <- as.numeric(pick_vig(d, "Sentence2", slider = TRUE))
# The two open-ends stay CHARACTER: they are the backward-looking justification
# and the forward-looking accomplishment item that E3-E7 score in
# 02_nlp_integration.Rmd. They are coalesced here only so the merged frame is
# complete; nothing in this document analyses their text.
if (!"Sentence_OpenEnd1" %in% names(d) && "Sentence_OpenEnd1_V1" %in% names(d))
  d$Sentence_OpenEnd1 <- pick_vig(d, "Sentence_OpenEnd1")
if (!"Sentence_OpenEnd2" %in% names(d) && "Sentence_OpenEnd2_V1" %in% names(d))
  d$Sentence_OpenEnd2 <- pick_vig(d, "Sentence_OpenEnd2")

# Friendly names for the slider exports
# Qualtrics appends _1 to every slider column, so the CRT items and age arrive
# as CRT_1_1, CRT_2_1, CRT_3_1, age_1. The third open-end, the ranking
# explanation, exports as `Priorit_Explain`; the pre-registration calls that
# item Q333 (Section 5.15).
if (!"CRT_1" %in% names(d) && "CRT_1_1" %in% names(d)) d$CRT_1 <- d$CRT_1_1
if (!"CRT_2" %in% names(d) && "CRT_2_1" %in% names(d)) d$CRT_2 <- d$CRT_2_1
if (!"CRT_3" %in% names(d) && "CRT_3_1" %in% names(d)) d$CRT_3 <- d$CRT_3_1
if (!"age"   %in% names(d) && "age_1"   %in% names(d)) d$age   <- d$age_1

# --- Reverse coding (higher = more of the named construct) -------------------
# The (R) items named across Sections 5.2 - 5.12. Each gets a NEW column with an
# _R suffix rather than being reversed in place, so the raw item survives and a
# double reversal is impossible: rev7(rev7(x)) == x, and an in-place scheme run
# twice would silently restore the original scores with no error.
#
# NOT IN THIS LIST, and deliberately so: Retribution_6 and Retribution_7. Those
# two items carry Qualtrics RecodeValues that already map their raw choice ids
# (19-25) onto 1-7 in the same direction as Retribution_1-5, so the Values
# export delivers them correctly keyed. Adding them here would reverse an item
# that needs no reversing and would pull down the retribution subscale's alpha.
rev_items <- c("punishmore_1", "parsimony_1", "parsimony_2", "severity_2",
               "dueprocess_2", "hate_2", "degrad_1", "prisonvi_1", "prisonvi_2",
               "harsh_2", "fear_1", "essential_3", "Society_1", "Society_2",
               "Society_3", "rwa_3", "sdo_3", "sdo_4", "sdo_7", "sdo_8",
               "Raceresent_1", "Raceresent_4")
for (it in intersect(rev_items, names(d))) d[[paste0(it, "_R")]] <- rev7(d[[it]])
# severity_1 is reversed ONLY for the just-deserts proportionality component.
# Section 5.4: proportionality is scored from the proportionality item together
# with the two severity items reverse-keyed, "so that wanting punishment greater
# or less than the crime lowers proportionality". Read on its own, severity_1
# ("punishment should exceed the seriousness of the crime") is a punitiveness
# item in the ordinary direction, and H4/H5 use it that way. Reversing the raw
# column instead of writing severity_1_R would flip its meaning everywhere.
if ("severity_1" %in% names(d)) d$severity_1_R <- rev7(d$severity_1)

# --- Within-vignette z-score of the first sentence --------------------------
# Section 5.11: "Because the three vignettes differ in severity, the first
# sentence is standardized within vignette before it is pooled or added to the
# punitiveness index." Standardizing within vignette removes the mean and spread
# differences the vignette manipulation creates, so a pooled Sentence1_z ranks a
# participant against the people who read the SAME case. Standardizing across
# the pooled sample instead would let vignette severity masquerade as
# individual punitiveness.
if (has_col(c("Sentence1", "Vignette"))) {
  d$Sentence1_z <- NA_real_
  # One pass per vignette, each writing into its own disjoint row slice.
  # na.omit() inside unique() keeps an unassigned row from creating a fourth
  # phantom group.
  for (v in sort(unique(stats::na.omit(d$Vignette)))) {
    sel <- !is.na(d$Vignette) & d$Vignette == v
    x   <- d$Sentence1[sel]
    d$Sentence1_z[sel] <- (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / stats::sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
}

# --- Composites (Sections 5.2 - 5.12) ---------------------------------------
# Reset the log before building, so re-running this chunk alone replaces the
# reliability rows rather than appending a second copy of each.
alpha_table <- data.frame()   # reset the log

# --- The four goals of punishment (Section 5.3) ------------------------------
# Retribution_1..7 spans the desert purpose items and the debt/unfair-advantage
# items; Retribution_1-4 alone are the "deserved" purpose items H6 uses.
d$retribution     <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Retribution_", 1:7), "retribution (7)")
d$deterrence      <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Deterrence_", 1:3), "deterrence")
d$incapacitation  <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Incapacitation_", 1:2), "incapacitation")
d$rehabilitation  <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Rehabilitation_", 1:2), "rehabilitation")
# E2's Durkheimian reading. Section 5.3 drops Solidarity_1 ("Removing criminals
# from society helps society cleanse itself") because it reads as EXCLUSIONARY
# rather than Durkheimian -- it describes purging the group, not binding the
# law-abiding together through a shared statement of norms. Leaving it in would
# load the Durkheimian composite with the very content the hostile composite
# measures and blunt the comparison E2 exists to make.
d$solidarity_durk <- compute_composite(d, c("Solidarity_2", "Solidarity_3"),
                                       "solidarity (Durkheimian, S2+S3)")
# All three items, built ONLY to serve the Phase 3 sensitivity check that puts
# Solidarity_1 back. Never the primary E2 measure.
d$solidarity_all  <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Solidarity_", 1:3),
                                       "solidarity (all 3, sensitivity only)")

# --- Punitiveness (Section 5.2) ---------------------------------------------
# The eight self-report items: two on punishing more, two parsimony items
# reversed, two three-strikes items, life without parole, and the death penalty.
punit_items <- c("punishmore_1_R", "punishmore_2", "parsimony_1_R", "parsimony_2_R",
                 "threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2", "LWOP", "deathpenalty")
d$punitiveness <- compute_composite(d, punit_items, "punitiveness (8-item self-report)")
# The FULL index adds the standardized sentence. It is built for completeness and
# is deliberately NOT used anywhere the sentence is on the other side of a test.
#
# HAZARD: punitiveness_full embeds Sentence1_z. Substituting it for
# `punitiveness` anywhere in Phase 5 (the sentence change), Phase 6 (the ratio x
# moderator models), or Phase 7 (measure agreement) would put the sentence on
# both sides of the same model and manufacture the association. Sections 5.3 and
# 5.11 both state the rule: wherever the sentencing ratio and punitiveness meet,
# use the sentence-free eight-item scale. The two are averaged AFTER scaling the
# self-report side, so the composite and the z-scored sentence carry equal
# weight rather than the sentence dominating on its wider raw range.
d$punitiveness_full <- rowMeans(cbind(as.numeric(scale(d$punitiveness)),
                                      d$Sentence1_z), na.rm = TRUE)

# --- Revenge, proportionality, just deserts (Section 5.4) -------------------
d$revenge            <- compute_composite(d, paste0("revenge_", 1:4), "revenge")
# Proportionality uses BOTH severity items reverse-keyed, so that wanting
# punishment greater than the crime (severity_1) or less than the harm
# (severity_2) each lowers the score. This is the only place severity_1_R is used.
d$proportionality_jd <- compute_composite(d, c("proportionality", "severity_1_R", "severity_2_R"),
                                          "proportionality (just-deserts)")
d$deserved           <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Retribution_", 1:4), "deserved (R1-R4)")
# Just deserts is the mean of its two halves rather than a pooled item mean, so
# the desert side and the proportionality side count equally regardless of how
# many items each contributes. H6 tests whether these two halves cohere at all;
# a near-zero correlation between them and a low alpha are the PREDICTED
# outcome, and the incoherence is itself the finding.
d$just_deserts       <- rowMeans(cbind(d$deserved, d$proportionality_jd), na.rm = TRUE)

# --- The Kantian limits (Section 5.5) ---------------------------------------
# Scored as WILLINGNESS TO SET THE LIMIT ASIDE, so a higher value is the less
# restrained, more punitive direction. dueprocess_2 protects the limit and is
# therefore the reversed item of the three.
d$dueprocess <- compute_composite(d, c("dueprocess_1", "dueprocess_2_R", "dueprocess_3"),
                                  "due process (permissive)")
d$uncertain  <- compute_composite(d, paste0("uncertain_", 1:4), "uncertain evidence")

# --- Emotions toward offenders (Section 5.7) --------------------------------
# Hatred belongs to the hostile-aggression cluster and also stands in, reversed,
# for dispassion among the Kantian limits.
d$hatred <- compute_composite(d, c("hate_1", "hate_2_R", "hate_3"), "hatred")
d$anger  <- compute_composite(d, paste0("anger_", 1:2), "anger")

# --- Harshness toward offenders (Section 5.8) -------------------------------
# degrad_1, prisonvi_1, and prisonvi_2 are worded as protections, hence reversed.
d$degradation <- compute_composite(d, c("degrad_1_R", "degrad_2", "degrad_3"), "degradation")
d$suffering   <- compute_composite(d, paste0("suffer_", 1:2), "infliction of suffering")
d$prisonviol  <- compute_composite(d, c("prisonvi_1_R", "prisonvi_2_R"), "prison-violence tolerance")
d$harsh       <- compute_composite(d, c("harsh_1", "harsh_2_R", "harsh_3"), "harsh conditions")

# --- Crime concerns (Section 5.6) -------------------------------------------
d$crimerates <- compute_composite(d, paste0("rates_", 1:2), "perceived crime rates")
d$fear       <- compute_composite(d, c("fear_1_R", "fear_2", "fear_3"), "fear of crime")

# --- Exclusion, essentialism, choice, society (Section 5.9) -----------------
# `exclusion` does double duty: E2's HOSTILE solidarity reading here, and the
# social-exclusion correlate in the H1 set. Section 5.3 forbids entering it
# twice in the same analysis, which is why Phase 4's correlate matrix and
# Phase 3's E2 test are separate analyses, never one pooled model.
d$exclusion      <- compute_composite(d, paste0("exclusion_", 1:3), "social exclusion (hostile solidarity)")
d$essentialism   <- compute_composite(d, c("essential_1", "essential_2", "essential_3_R", "essential_4"), "essentialism")
d$choice         <- compute_composite(d, paste0("choice_", 1:2), "crime as choice")
d$society_reject <- compute_composite(d, c("Society_1_R", "Society_2_R", "Society_3_R"),
                                      "society responsibility (rejected)")

# --- Personality and cognitive reflection (Section 5.12) --------------------
# These five are the E1 outcomes. Reversal keys follow the published scales:
# rwa_3 for the five-item RWA, and sdo_3/4/7/8 for the eight-item SDO7 short
# form, whose second four items are the pro-equality subscale.
d$rwa        <- compute_composite(d, c("rwa_1", "rwa_2", "rwa_3_R", "rwa_4", "rwa_5"), "RWA")
d$sdo        <- compute_composite(d, c("sdo_1", "sdo_2", "sdo_3_R", "sdo_4_R",
                                       "sdo_5", "sdo_6", "sdo_7_R", "sdo_8_R"), "SDO7")
d$vprone     <- compute_composite(d, paste0("vprone_", 1:4), "violence proneness")
# Racial resentment: Raceresent_1 and _4 are the sympathy/discrimination items,
# reversed so that higher means more resentment.
d$raceresent <- compute_composite(d, c("Raceresent_1_R", "Raceresent_2",
                                       "Raceresent_3", "Raceresent_4_R"), "racial resentment")

# CRT scored 0-3; correct answers are 5 cents, 5 minutes, 47 days.
# The three standard items and their INTUITIVE-but-wrong lures: the bat and ball
# costs $1.10 and the ball is 5 cents (the lure is 10); 100 machines take the
# same 5 minutes as 5 machines (the lure is 100); a patch that doubles daily and
# covers the lake on day 48 covered half on day 47 (the lure is 24). Scoring is
# the NUMBER CORRECT, so higher = more reflective, which is why E1 predicts
# retributivists score LOWER here while scoring higher on the other four.
# Sums of logicals coerce to integer, giving 0-3 directly. Note this is a strict
# equality test on slider values, so a participant who typed "0.05" for five
# cents rather than "5" registers as incorrect -- the item asks for cents and
# the slider is labelled in cents.
if (has_col(c("CRT_1", "CRT_2", "CRT_3")))
  d$CRT <- (d$CRT_1 == 5) + (d$CRT_2 == 5) + (d$CRT_3 == 47)

# Cluster aggregates (mean of z-scored constituents)
# z-scoring FIRST is what makes these means meaningful: the constituents are on
# the same 1-7 scale but with very different spreads, and an unstandardized mean
# would silently weight the widest-spread component most. hostile_agg is the
# hostile-aggression cluster H2 contrasts with crime_concerns; both appear here
# as correlates and moderator outcomes, not as confirmatory tests.
zc <- function(...) rowMeans(scale(cbind(...)), na.rm = TRUE)
d$hostile_agg    <- zc(d$hatred, d$revenge, d$degradation, d$suffering, d$prisonviol)
d$crime_concerns <- zc(d$crimerates, d$fear)

cat(sprintf("Rebuilt %d composites. Reliability log has %d rows.\n",
            nrow(alpha_table), nrow(alpha_table)))
show_table(alpha_table[, c("composite", "k", "alpha", "omega")],
           caption = "Reliability of the composites used in this document")
```

## 1.3 The retributivist measures (Section 5.3)

```{r phase1_retributivist}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 1.3 — THE RETRIBUTIVIST MEASURES (Section 5.3)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds the three survey-based definitions of
# retributivism and the grouping factors every contrast below uses.
#
# WHY MORE THAN ONE: Section 5.3 expects any single measure, and any self-report
# measure in particular, to be imperfect -- demand characteristics push
# participants toward the forward-looking justifications, intuitive
# retributivism means people punish on desert while describing utilitarian
# aims, and introspective access to punitive motive is limited. So the plan
# fixes three measures plus an exploratory fourth, and requires "every contrast
# under each measure rather than only the one that gives the strongest result."
# That is why Phase 2 runs E1 four times over.
#
# OBJECTS CREATED: retributivist, retribution_rel, retrib_medsplit,
#   retrib_tertile, sentence_ratio, ratio_medsplit, and the grp_* factors.
# ===========================================================================

# (1) RANKING — the primary categorical definition. Prioritization_1 is the rank
#     given to "Criminals deserve to be punished"; == 1 means ranked first.
# Participants rank all four goals, so this is a forced choice among them rather
# than an endorsement rating: it identifies people who put desert ABOVE
# deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation, not merely people who agree
# with desert. as.integer() gives the 0/1 coding grp_rank expects.
if ("Prioritization_1" %in% names(d))
  d$retributivist <- as.integer(d$Prioritization_1 == 1)

# (2) RELATIVE RETRIBUTION SUBSCALE — the primary continuous measure:
#     retribution minus the mean of the other three goals.
# Section 5.3 defines it as retribution with the other three partialled out,
# "equivalently, retribution minus the mean of the other three". Subtracting the
# mean of the rivals is what captures PRIORITIZING retribution rather than
# simply endorsing every goal: an acquiescent participant who rates all four
# goals a 7 scores 0 here, while the raw retribution subscale would put them at
# the ceiling. This is the measure used wherever retributivism enters as a
# continuous predictor.
d$retribution_rel <- d$retribution -
  rowMeans(cbind(d$deterrence, d$incapacitation, d$rehabilitation), na.rm = TRUE)

# Section 5.3 asks for a median split "with the top and bottom thirds alongside
# it", so both are built. The median split keeps the whole sample and the power
# that comes with it; the tertile contrast trades sample size for separation
# between the compared groups. Reporting both is the point -- a result that
# appears only under one of them is a result that depends on the cut.
rel_split <- balanced_split(d$retribution_rel)
d$retrib_medsplit <- rel_split$split
tert <- stats::quantile(d$retribution_rel, c(1/3, 2/3), na.rm = TRUE)
# The -Inf and Inf sentinels make the outer bins open-ended so no value falls
# outside all breaks and becomes NA. The middle third is retained as "mid" here
# and dropped only when grp_tert is built below.
d$retrib_tertile <- cut(d$retribution_rel, c(-Inf, tert, Inf),
                        labels = c("low", "mid", "high"))

# (3) SENTENCING RATIO — the behavioral measure: share of the first sentence
#     retained in the second, for participants whose first sentence was above 0.
# Section 5.11: once the added facts remove the forward-looking reasons (the
# defendant is permanently disabled and no longer a danger, and procedural rules
# remove any prospect of general deterrence), whatever punishment a participant
# still imposes reflects desert. A HIGHER ratio means a SMALLER reduction and so
# a more retributive motive.
#
# The Sentence1 > 0 guard is not cosmetic: a first sentence of zero would make
# the ratio a division by zero, and a participant who imposed no punishment at
# all has no proportion to retain. Those rows become NA and drop out pairwise.
d$sentence_ratio <- ifelse(!is.na(d$Sentence1) & d$Sentence1 > 0,
                           d$Sentence2 / d$Sentence1, NA_real_)
# The ratio piles up at exactly 1.0 (no reduction at all), so a strict
# "above the median" split is degenerate. balanced_split() falls back to
# "at or above the median", which here separates the participants who kept the
# whole sentence from those who cut it — the substantive contrast Section 5.11
# describes ("a higher ratio, meaning a smaller reduction").
ratio_split <- balanced_split(d$sentence_ratio)
d$ratio_medsplit <- ratio_split$split

# --- Grouping factors used by every contrast in this document ---------------
# CRITICAL ORDERING RULE: in every factor below, the LOW level is listed first.
# welch_contrast() computes t and Cohen's d as level 2 minus level 1, so this
# ordering is what makes every reported d read "high retributivism minus low".
# Swapping a levels= argument here would flip the sign of every effect in the
# document without raising a single warning.
d$grp_rank  <- factor(d$retributivist,    levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("non-retributivist", "retributivist"))
d$grp_rel   <- factor(d$retrib_medsplit,  levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("rel. subscale low", "rel. subscale high"))
# The middle third becomes NA here, so grp_tert has exactly two populated levels
# and welch_contrast() compares only the extremes. droplevels() inside that
# helper removes the emptied level before the nlevels() == 2 check.
d$grp_tert  <- factor(ifelse(d$retrib_tertile == "low", "bottom third",
                      ifelse(d$retrib_tertile == "high", "top third", NA)),
                      levels = c("bottom third", "top third"))
# The labels spell out the direction because the ratio inverts the usual
# intuition: a HIGH ratio means the participant cut LESS, which is the more
# retributive side.
d$grp_ratio <- factor(d$ratio_medsplit,   levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("ratio low (larger reduction)",
                                 "ratio high (smaller reduction)"))

cat(sprintf("Retributivists by RANKING: %d of %d (%s)\n",
            sum(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(d$retributivist)),
            pct(mean(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE))))
cat(sprintf("Relative retribution subscale: M = %.2f, SD = %.2f, median = %.2f\n",
            mean(d$retribution_rel, na.rm = TRUE),
            stats::sd(d$retribution_rel, na.rm = TRUE), rel_split$cut))
cat(sprintf("  split rule: %s -> %d high, %d low\n", rel_split$rule,
            sum(d$retrib_medsplit == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(d$retrib_medsplit == 0, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Sentencing ratio: median = %.2f, n with Sentence1 > 0 = %d\n",
            ratio_split$cut, sum(!is.na(d$sentence_ratio))))
cat(sprintf("  ratio exactly 1.00 (no reduction): %d participants\n",
            sum(d$sentence_ratio == 1, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("  split rule: %s -> %d high, %d low\n", ratio_split$rule,
            sum(d$ratio_medsplit == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(d$ratio_medsplit == 0, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat("\nTertile split on the relative subscale:\n")
print(table(d$retrib_tertile, useNA = "ifany"))
```

## 1.4 The semantic measure (exploratory, Section 5.3 / 6.7)

The fourth retributivist definition is the **semantic measure**: the retributive
facets scored from the open-ended responses by the language-model ensemble
described in Section 6.7. Section 6.7 makes that ensemble's output usable only
after a validation gate — an intraclass correlation of at least .60 across
models, and a correlation of at least .30 with the matching survey scale — and
`02_nlp_integration.Rmd` owns both the ensemble and the gate.

Until a facet clears that gate, this document treats the semantic measure as a
**placeholder**. If the dictionary (word-list) facet scores are on disk, they
are loaded as a clearly labelled **provisional stand-in** so that the agreement
analysis in Phase 7 has something to display. The word list is one of the two
non-model safeguards Section 6.7 names, which makes it a defensible stand-in —
its agreement with the ensemble is a more independent check than the models'
agreement with one another — but it is not the semantic measure itself, and
nothing in this document should be read as if it were. Substituting a validated
ensemble score is a change to this one chunk.

```{r phase1_semantic}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 1.4 — THE SEMANTIC MEASURE (exploratory, Sections 5.3 and 6.7)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: attempts to attach a semantic retributivism score to
# each participant, and records in SEMANTIC_STATUS exactly what was attached.
#
# OBJECTS CREATED: semantic_retributivism, sem_medsplit, grp_sem,
#   SEMANTIC_STATUS (a string printed wherever this measure is used).
#
# DESIGN RULE: this chunk NEVER silently upgrades a stand-in into the real
# measure. SEMANTIC_STATUS travels with every table built from it, so a reader
# of Phase 2.4 or Phase 7 always sees which of the two they are looking at.
# ===========================================================================

# Default state: no measure. Every downstream chunk is written to handle it, so
# the document knits whether or not the NLP outputs are on disk.
SEMANTIC_STATUS <- "placeholder (no measure available)"
d$semantic_retributivism <- NA_real_

# ResponseId is the merge key; if 01's output somehow lacks it there is nothing
# to join on, so the placeholder stands.
if (file.exists(SEMANTIC_CSV) && "ResponseId" %in% names(d)) {
  # tryCatch rather than a bare read: a partially written or malformed file from
  # the NLP side should leave the placeholder in place, not abort the knit.
  sem <- tryCatch(
    readr::read_csv(SEMANTIC_CSV, show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 10000),
    error = function(e) NULL)

  # === COVERAGE GUARD ===
  # The facet file has to describe the sample being analysed. A file scored on a
  # different (for instance earlier and smaller) download would merge cleanly on
  # ResponseId and produce a measure computed on whoever happened to overlap,
  # reported beside statistics based on the full analytic sample. That is a
  # silent sample swap, and nothing downstream would reveal it, so the coverage
  # is checked here and the measure is refused rather than computed on a
  # fraction. SEMANTIC_MIN_COVERAGE is the share of the analytic sample the file
  # must cover; 0.9 allows for participants who simply wrote nothing.
  SEMANTIC_MIN_COVERAGE <- 0.90
  if (!is.null(sem) && "response_id" %in% names(sem)) {
    sem_ids   <- unique(sem$response_id)
    sem_cover <- length(intersect(sem_ids, d$ResponseId)) / nrow(d)
    cat(sprintf("Facet file covers %d of the %d analysed participants (%.1f%%).\n",
                length(intersect(sem_ids, d$ResponseId)), nrow(d), 100 * sem_cover))
    if (sem_cover < SEMANTIC_MIN_COVERAGE) {
      cat(sprintf(paste0("Coverage is below the %.0f%% floor, so the semantic ",
                         "stand-in is NOT computed. Re-score the open-ends on ",
                         "the current export in Colab NB01 and place the fresh ",
                         "facet_dictionary_scores.csv in Analysis/NLP/outputs/.\n"),
                  100 * SEMANTIC_MIN_COVERAGE))
      sem <- NULL
    }
  }

  # The four PRINCIPLED facets of Section 5.15: desert (the offender earned it),
  # proportionality (a punishment that fits and no more), censure (punishment as
  # a statement that the act was wrong), and moral balance (paying a debt).
  # The two harder-edged facets, revenge and suffering, are deliberately NOT
  # averaged in here -- E4 asks whether the two sets co-occur, so folding them
  # into one score would destroy the distinction the study exists to test.
  # The _per100 suffix means hits per 100 words, which is the word list's own
  # length normalization.
  needed <- c("response_id", "item_type",
              "desert_per100", "proportionality_per100",
              "censure_per100", "moral_balance_per100")

  # all() of the required columns: a file with the right name but the wrong
  # schema leaves the placeholder standing rather than producing a half-scored
  # measure.
  if (!is.null(sem) && all(needed %in% names(sem))) {
    # BACKWARD-looking texts only: the sentence justification and the ranking
    # explanation. The forward-looking item is excluded by design (Section 5.15).
    # Those two items ask what the offender did; the accomplishment item asks
    # what the sentence should achieve, which is where consequentialist language
    # naturally lives. Pooling all three would mix the two kinds of reasoning
    # that E6 is built to separate, and would understate retributive content for
    # anyone who wrote at length about deterrence in the forward item.
    sem_bw <- sem[sem$item_type %in% c("backward", "ranking"), , drop = FALSE]
    sem_bw$principled <- rowMeans(
      sem_bw[, c("desert_per100", "proportionality_per100",
                 "censure_per100", "moral_balance_per100")], na.rm = TRUE)

    # The NLP file is LONG (one row per participant per open-end), so aggregate
    # to one score per participant before merging into the wide survey frame.
    # Averaging the two backward texts gives each participant equal weight
    # regardless of how many of the two they answered substantively.
    agg <- stats::aggregate(principled ~ response_id, data = sem_bw,
                            FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    names(agg) <- c("ResponseId", "semantic_provisional")
    # all.x = TRUE is a LEFT join: participants without a scored open-end keep
    # every other variable and simply get NA here. sort = FALSE preserves row
    # order, which matters because Sentence1_z and the grp_* factors were
    # already computed against this frame's current ordering.
    d <- merge(d, agg, by = "ResponseId", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
    d$semantic_retributivism <- d$semantic_provisional

    # The status string is deliberately blunt. It is printed above the Phase 2.4
    # contrast table and inside the Phase 7 measure-status table.
    SEMANTIC_STATUS <- paste0(
```
