```{r phase1_semantic}
      "PROVISIONAL word-list stand-in (dictionary facets, backward-looking ",
      "texts); NOT the validated LLM-ensemble semantic measure")
  }
}

# Dichotomize the same way as the other two continuous definitions, so the four
# E1 contrasts differ in their measure and not in how the cut was made.
n_sem <- sum(!is.na(d$semantic_retributivism))
if (n_sem > 0) {
  sem_split <- balanced_split(d$semantic_retributivism)
  d$sem_medsplit <- sem_split$split
  d$grp_sem <- factor(d$sem_medsplit, levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("semantic low", "semantic high"))
} else {
  # An all-NA factor WITH the two levels declared. This is what lets
  # run_contrasts() reach welch_contrast(), fail its nlevels() check, and return
  # NULL cleanly; a bare NA column would error on droplevels() instead.
  d$sem_medsplit <- NA_integer_
  d$grp_sem <- factor(rep(NA_character_, nrow(d)),
                      levels = c("semantic low", "semantic high"))
}

cat(sprintf("Semantic measure status: %s\n", SEMANTIC_STATUS))
cat(sprintf("Participants with a semantic score: %d of %d\n", n_sem, nrow(d)))
if (n_sem > 0) print(summary(d$semantic_retributivism))
```

# PHASE 2: E1 — PERSONALITY AND COGNITIVE REFLECTION BETWEEN GROUPS

**E1.** Retributivists score higher than non-retributivists on RWA, SDO,
violence proneness, and racial resentment, and lower on cognitive reflection.

Section 6.6 says E1 uses "the same methods" as the confirmatory group contrasts,
which Section 6.5 fixes as Welch t-tests with Cohen's d, run under each
retributivist definition (Section 5.3 requires "every contrast under each
measure rather than only the one that gives the strongest result"), plus a
continuous regression so the result does not depend on a split.

```{r phase2_setup}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 2.0 — E1 SPECIFICATION
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: fixes the five E1 outcomes and, for each, the direction
# the prediction names. Nothing is estimated here; declaring the directions in
# one place is what keeps the one-sided tests below honest, because the
# direction is set before any contrast is run rather than read off the result.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: E1 (Section 2.4), tested by the methods of Sections 6.5 and 6.6.
# OBJECTS CREATED: e1_vars, e1_labels, e1_dir -- all consumed by 2.1 through 2.5.
# ===========================================================================

# intersect() rather than a bare vector, so a missing personality scale drops
# the row instead of erroring five chunks later.
e1_vars <- intersect(c("rwa", "sdo", "vprone", "raceresent", "CRT"), names(d))
e1_labels <- c(rwa = "Right-Wing Authoritarianism", sdo = "Social Dominance (SDO7)",
               vprone = "Violence proneness", raceresent = "Racial resentment",
               CRT = "Cognitive Reflection (0-3)")

# Predicted direction for the HIGH-retributivism group.
# E1 names a direction for all five outcomes, so all five get a one-sided test
# in the predicted direction under Section 6.8 ("Predictions that name a
# direction are tested one-sided in that direction; the rest are two-sided").
# CRT is the odd one out at "less": the CRT is scored as the NUMBER CORRECT, so
# a higher score means MORE reflection, and E1 predicts retributivists are less
# reflective. Flipping this entry to "greater" would test the opposite claim
# while still printing a plausible-looking p-value.
# The two-sided p is reported alongside in every table, so a reader who prefers
# the conservative convention has it without recomputing anything.
e1_dir <- list(rwa = "greater", sdo = "greater", vprone = "greater",
               raceresent = "greater", CRT = "less")

cat("E1 outcome variables and predicted direction for the high group:\n")
for (v in e1_vars)
  cat(sprintf("  %-12s %-32s %s\n", v, e1_labels[[v]], e1_dir[[v]]))
```

## 2.1 E1 under the ranking definition (primary categorical)

```{r phase2_e1_ranking}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 2.1 — E1 UNDER THE RANKING DEFINITION
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The PRIMARY categorical grouping (Section 5.3): participants who ranked
# "criminals deserve to be punished" first versus everyone else. Welch t-tests
# with Cohen's d, one-sided in the direction E1 names.
#
# PRODUCES: `e1_rank`, reused by the Phase 2.5 combined CSV and the Phase 8.3
# response-quality sensitivity comparison; and the printed contrast table.
#
# `df` is displayed here (and only here) because this is the primary contrast:
# its fractional value is the visible signature of the Welch correction.
# NO FDR ADJUSTMENT is applied across the five rows. Section 6.6 places E1
# outside both preregistered families, and the five personality outcomes were
# never declared as a family of their own; pooling them into a BH sweep would
# invent a family the plan does not contain.
# ===========================================================================
e1_rank <- run_contrasts(d, e1_vars, "grp_rank", e1_dir,
                         label = "ranking (retribution 1st)")
show_table(pick_cols(e1_rank, c("variable", "n_low", "n_high", "M_low", "M_high",
                       "t", "df", "p_two_sided", "p_directional",
                       "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
           caption = "E1 — ranking definition: Welch t-tests and Cohen's d")
```

## 2.2 E1 under the relative retribution subscale

Section 5.3 asks for a median split on the relative subscale, "with the top and
bottom thirds alongside it."

```{r phase2_e1_relative}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 2.2 — E1 UNDER THE RELATIVE RETRIBUTION SUBSCALE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The same five outcomes and the same one-sided directions, now split on the
# PRIMARY CONTINUOUS measure. Two cuts, exactly as Section 5.3 asks:
#   - median split, which keeps all 948 participants and the power that buys;
#   - top versus bottom third, which discards the middle third to widen the gap
#     between the compared groups at the cost of a third of the sample.
# Neither is privileged. Reading them together is the point: an effect that
# appears under one cut and not the other is an effect that depends on the cut,
# and the continuous regression in 2.5 is the arbiter that needs no cut at all.
#
# PRODUCES: `e1_rel`, `e1_tert`, both stacked into the Phase 2.5 CSV and figure.
# ===========================================================================
e1_rel  <- run_contrasts(d, e1_vars, "grp_rel",  e1_dir,
                         label = "relative subscale (median split)")
e1_tert <- run_contrasts(d, e1_vars, "grp_tert", e1_dir,
                         label = "relative subscale (top vs bottom third)")

show_table(pick_cols(e1_rel, c("variable", "n_low", "n_high", "M_low", "M_high",
                      "t", "p_two_sided", "p_directional", "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
           caption = "E1 — relative retribution subscale, median split")
show_table(pick_cols(e1_tert, c("variable", "n_low", "n_high", "M_low", "M_high",
                       "t", "p_two_sided", "p_directional", "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
           caption = "E1 — relative retribution subscale, top vs bottom third")
```

## 2.3 E1 under the sentencing ratio

The sentencing ratio is a legitimate grouping variable for E1: none of the E1
outcomes is the sentence, so the circularity restriction in Section 5.3 does not
bite here.

```{r phase2_e1_ratio}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 2.3 — E1 UNDER THE SENTENCING RATIO
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The BEHAVIORAL definition, and the one Section 5.3 suspects "may prove the
# sharpest of the measures" because it registers a retributive motive from what
# a participant DOES rather than from what they report.
#
# WHY IT IS ALLOWED HERE AND FORBIDDEN IN PHASE 5: Section 5.3 lists the
# personality measures (E1) among the outcomes the ratio may group, and rules it
# out only for the sentence-based hypothesis H14, "because it is built from the
# same sentence H14 tests." RWA, SDO, violence proneness, racial resentment, and
# the CRT are all measured well before the sentencing vignette, so no part of
# the grouping variable appears on the outcome side. Phase 5.2 faces the
# opposite situation and drops the ratio as a grouping variable accordingly.
#
# The high group is the SMALLER reduction, so the E1 directions carry over
# unchanged: high ratio = more retributive.
# PRODUCES: `e1_ratio`.
# ===========================================================================
e1_ratio <- run_contrasts(d, e1_vars, "grp_ratio", e1_dir,
                          label = "sentencing ratio (median split)")
show_table(pick_cols(e1_ratio, c("variable", "n_low", "n_high", "M_low", "M_high",
                        "t", "p_two_sided", "p_directional", "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
           caption = "E1 — sentencing ratio, median split (high ratio = smaller drop)")
```

## 2.4 E1 under the semantic measure

```{r phase2_e1_semantic}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 2.4 — E1 UNDER THE SEMANTIC MEASURE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The fourth and most exploratory definition. Whether anything prints at all
# depends on Phase 1.4: with no scores attached, grp_sem is an all-NA factor,
# welch_contrast() fails its nlevels() check, run_contrasts() returns NULL, and
# the chunk reports the placeholder status instead of a table.
#
# The `if` is on run_contrasts()'s return value rather than on SEMANTIC_STATUS,
# so the branch follows what was actually estimable rather than what was
# intended. Where a table DOES print, SEMANTIC_STATUS is printed directly above
# it, because a word-list stand-in and a validated ensemble score would produce
# tables that look identical and mean quite different things.
#
# Note the restriction that does NOT apply here: Section 5.3 bars the semantic
# measure from grouping participants for the language hypotheses E3-E7, since
# those are built from the same responses. E1's outcomes are survey scales, so
# the restriction does not reach this contrast.
# PRODUCES: `e1_sem` (often NULL).
# ===========================================================================
e1_sem <- run_contrasts(d, e1_vars, "grp_sem", e1_dir,
                        label = "semantic measure (median split)")
if (is.null(e1_sem)) {
  cat("No semantic measure available — this contrast is a placeholder.\n")
  cat("Status:", SEMANTIC_STATUS, "\n")
} else {
  cat("NOTE:", SEMANTIC_STATUS, "\n\n")
  show_table(pick_cols(e1_sem, c("variable", "n_low", "n_high", "M_low", "M_high",
                        "t", "p_two_sided", "p_directional", "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
             caption = "E1 — semantic measure, median split (provisional)")
}
```

## 2.5 E1 with retributivism entered continuously

```{r phase2_e1_continuous}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 2.5 — E1 WITH RETRIBUTIVISM ENTERED CONTINUOUSLY
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: refits every E1 outcome on each continuous retributivism
# index with no split at all, then stacks all four grouped contrasts and writes
# both tables to output/tables/.
#
# WHY: Section 6.5 requires that "every group contrast" also be run "with
# retributivism entered continuously, as a regression on the retribution
# subscale, so the result does not depend on the split." Any median split throws
# away information and makes the estimate hostage to where the cut fell; these
# regressions are the version with no cut to argue about. Where a d in 2.1-2.4
# and a beta here disagree, the split is doing the work.
#
# PRODUCES: e1_cont, e1_all; output/tables/E1_personality_contrasts.csv and
#           output/tables/E1_personality_continuous.csv.
# ===========================================================================

# Standardized simple regressions: outcome ~ continuous retributivism index.
# The ranking is absent from this list by construction -- it is binary, so its
# "continuous" version is the Phase 2.1 contrast itself.
cont_predictors <- intersect(c("retribution_rel", "sentence_ratio",
                               "semantic_retributivism"), names(d))

# Nested lapply over outcomes x predictors, rbind-ed into one long table.
e1_cont <- do.call(rbind, lapply(e1_vars, function(v) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(cont_predictors, function(p) {
    # LISTWISE per pair. Subsetting to `ok` BEFORE scale() matters: scale()
    # computes its mean and SD from whatever it is handed, so standardizing the
    # full column and then dropping rows would leave the analysed subset with a
    # mean that is not zero, and beta would no longer be the correlation.
    ok <- stats::complete.cases(d[[v]], d[[p]])
    # Guards: too few pairs for a stable slope, or a constant on either side
    # (the semantic placeholder is constant when unavailable).
    if (sum(ok) < 10 || stats::sd(d[[p]][ok]) == 0 || stats::sd(d[[v]][ok]) == 0)
      return(NULL)
    # Both sides standardized, so the slope IS the standardized beta, which for
    # a single predictor equals the Pearson r. That makes these directly
    # comparable across outcomes measured on different scales (CRT is 0-3, the
    # personality composites are 1-7).
    fit <- stats::lm(scale(d[[v]][ok]) ~ scale(d[[p]][ok]))
    s   <- summary(fit)$coefficients
    ci  <- stats::confint(fit)
    # Row 2 of the coefficient matrix throughout: row 1 is the intercept, which
    # is zero by construction once both sides are standardized.
    # Only the two-sided p is reported here. The directional halving rule lives
    # in welch_contrast() and is not reapplied to the regressions, so a reader
    # comparing a beta with its matching d is comparing the conservative p in
    # both cases; halve it by hand if E1's direction is the one being tested.
    data.frame(outcome = v, predictor = p, n = sum(ok),
               beta = s[2, 1], se = s[2, 2], t = s[2, 3],
               p_two_sided = s[2, 4],
               ci_lo = ci[2, 1], ci_hi = ci[2, 2],
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}))

show_table(e1_cont,
           caption = "E1 — standardized regressions on the continuous retributivism measures")

# Stack all four grouped contrasts into one object for the CSV and the figure.
# Filter(Negate(is.null), ...) drops any definition that produced nothing --
# typically e1_sem -- because rbind() on a list containing NULL silently yields
# a shorter result and would misalign nothing here, but the explicit filter also
# keeps `e1_all` NULL rather than zero-row when every contrast failed.
e1_all <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null),
                                list(e1_rank, e1_rel, e1_tert, e1_ratio, e1_sem)))
if (!is.null(e1_all)) {
  readr::write_csv(e1_all, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "E1_personality_contrasts.csv"))
  cat("\nWrote output/tables/E1_personality_contrasts.csv\n")
}
if (!is.null(e1_cont)) {
  readr::write_csv(e1_cont, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "E1_personality_continuous.csv"))
  cat("Wrote output/tables/E1_personality_continuous.csv\n")
}
```

```{r phase2_e1_figure, fig.height=6}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 2.6 — E1 FOREST PLOT
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One panel showing Cohen's d with its 95% CI for every E1 outcome under every
# retributivist definition. The figure exists to make the convergence question
# visible at a glance: five outcomes x four definitions is twenty numbers, and
# the substantive question is whether the definitions agree on sign and rough
# magnitude, not whether any single cell clears .05.
#
# PRODUCES: output/figures/E1_personality_effects.png.
# ===========================================================================
if (!is.null(e1_all) && nrow(e1_all)) {
  plot_df <- e1_all
  # rev() because ggplot draws the first factor level at the BOTTOM of a
  # discrete y axis; reversing puts the outcomes in e1_vars order top to bottom,
  # matching the tables above.
  plot_df$variable <- factor(plot_df$variable, levels = rev(e1_vars))
  p_e1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df,
                          ggplot2::aes(x = d, y = variable, colour = grouping)) +
    # Reference line at d = 0, the no-difference point. An interval crossing it
    # is the visual equivalent of a two-sided test failing at alpha = .05.
    ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    # Horizontal CI bars, dodged so the four definitions for one outcome sit as
    # a legible stack rather than overprinting one another.
    ggplot2::geom_errorbarh(ggplot2::aes(xmin = d_lo, xmax = d_hi),
                            height = 0.18,
                            position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    # Same dodge width as the bars, so each point stays centred on its interval.
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.4,
                        position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = "E1: personality and cognitive reflection, high vs. low retributivism",
      subtitle = "Cohen's d (high minus low) with 95% CI, under each retributivist definition",
      x = "Cohen's d", y = NULL, colour = "Definition") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  print(p_e1)
  ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "E1_personality_effects.png"),
                  p_e1, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 150)
  cat("Saved: output/figures/E1_personality_effects.png\n")
}
```

# PHASE 3: E2 — HOSTILE VS. DURKHEIMIAN SOLIDARITY (STEIGER'S TEST)

**E2.** Hostile solidarity (social exclusion of offenders) relates to
punitiveness more strongly than Durkheimian solidarity (punishment as expressing
shared norms and binding the law-abiding together).

Two things fix the specification. First, Section 5.3 drops `Solidarity_1`
("Removing criminals from society helps society cleanse itself") from the
Durkheimian reading because it reads as exclusionary; the Durkheimian composite
is `Solidarity_2` + `Solidarity_3` only. Second, the punitiveness measure is the
**8-item self-report scale**, not the full index: nothing here needs the
sentence, and the self-report scale keeps the comparison clean.

The two correlations share `punitiveness`, so they are dependent and
**overlapping** — Steiger's (1980) test, one-sided in the predicted direction.

```{r phase3_e2_components}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 3.1 — E2 COMPONENT DESCRIPTIVES
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: prints the composition of the E2 measures and their n,
# mean, and SD, so the correlations in 3.2 can be read against the spread that
# produced them. A composite with almost no variance can only produce a small r
# whatever the underlying relationship, and the reader needs to see that first.
#
# `solidarity_all` appears here even though it is not part of E2 proper: it is
# the sensitivity composite Phase 3.3 uses, and showing its descriptives beside
# solidarity_durk makes visible how much adding Solidarity_1 moves the scale.
# ===========================================================================
cat("E2 components:\n")
cat("  hostile solidarity   = exclusion (exclusion_1..3)\n")
cat("  Durkheimian solidarity = solidarity_durk (Solidarity_2, Solidarity_3)\n")
cat("  Solidarity_1 is DROPPED per Section 5.3 (exclusionary, not Durkheimian)\n\n")

e2_desc <- data.frame(
  measure = c("punitiveness (8-item)", "exclusion (hostile)",
              "solidarity_durk (Durkheimian)", "solidarity_all (sensitivity)"),
  n  = sapply(c("punitiveness", "exclusion", "solidarity_durk", "solidarity_all"),
              function(v) sum(!is.na(d[[v]]))),
  M  = sapply(c("punitiveness", "exclusion", "solidarity_durk", "solidarity_all"),
              function(v) mean(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)),
  SD = sapply(c("punitiveness", "exclusion", "solidarity_durk", "solidarity_all"),
              function(v) stats::sd(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
show_table(e2_desc, caption = "E2 — component descriptives")
```

```{r phase3_e2_test}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 3.2 — E2: STEIGER'S TEST
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reports the three correlations that enter Steiger's test
# individually, then the test itself.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: E2 (Section 2.4), by the method Section 6.6 specifies.
#
# WHY ALL THREE r's ARE SHOWN FIRST: the test's verdict depends on r(hostile,
# Durkheimian) as much as on the two focal coefficients. Two competitors that
# are themselves highly correlated share most of their sampling error, so even a
# large gap between them can fail to reach significance; two that are nearly
# independent can separate on a smaller gap. Printing r_between makes that
# visible instead of leaving the reader to wonder why a difference of a given
# size did or did not clear alpha.
#
# WHY ONE-SIDED: E2 names a direction ("more strongly than"), so Section 6.8
# puts it one-sided in that direction. alternative = "greater" tests
# r(punitiveness, hostile) > r(punitiveness, Durkheimian); a result in the
# opposite direction returns a p above .5 rather than a small one, which is the
# correct behaviour for a directional prediction that failed.
#
# PRODUCES: `e2` (list) and `e2_tab`, both reused by the Phase 3.3 spec table.
# ===========================================================================

# The three coefficients with their 95% CIs, per Section 6.8's requirement that
# every test report an effect size and an interval.
e2_cors <- rbind(
  c(pair = NA, get_cor_ci("punitiveness", "exclusion", d)),
  c(pair = NA, get_cor_ci("punitiveness", "solidarity_durk", d)),
  c(pair = NA, get_cor_ci("exclusion",    "solidarity_durk", d))
)
# get_cor_ci() returns a numeric vector, so a character label cannot be rbind-ed
# alongside it without coercing everything to character. The placeholder column
# is therefore created as NA, dropped by [, -1], and the labels attached after
# the frame exists.
e2_cors <- as.data.frame(e2_cors[, -1, drop = FALSE])
e2_cors$pair <- c("punitiveness x hostile solidarity",
                  "punitiveness x Durkheimian solidarity",
                  "hostile x Durkheimian solidarity")
e2_cors <- e2_cors[, c("pair", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p", "n")]
show_table(e2_cors, caption = "E2 — the three correlations entering Steiger's test")

# `punitiveness` is the SHARED variable j, which is what makes these two
# correlations overlapping rather than merely dependent.
#
# HAZARD: this must be the 8-item self-report punitiveness scale, not
# punitiveness_full. Nothing in E2 needs the sentence, and swapping in the full
# index would drag Sentence1_z into both coefficients and change what the test
# is comparing.
e2 <- steiger_overlap(d, "punitiveness", "exclusion", "solidarity_durk",
                      alternative = "greater")
e2_tab <- if (is.null(e2)) NULL else e2$table

show_table(e2_tab, caption = "E2 — Steiger's test (one-sided: hostile > Durkheimian)")

if (is.null(e2_tab)) {
  cat("Steiger's test could not be computed (insufficient complete cases).\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "r(punitiveness, hostile) = %.3f vs r(punitiveness, Durkheimian) = %.3f\n",
    e2_tab$r_1, e2_tab$r_2))
  cat(sprintf("difference = %.3f, Steiger z = %.3f, one-sided p %s\n",
              e2_tab$diff, e2_tab$steiger_z, format_p(e2_tab$p)))
  # alpha = .05 is the Section 6.8 threshold. The verdict is worded "in this
  # sample" because E2 is exploratory: Section 6.6 keeps it out of the
  # confirmatory machinery, so a small p here marks a claim worth testing
  # confirmatorily in a future study rather than an established effect.
  cat(sprintf("Conclusion at alpha = .05: E2 %s\n",
              ifelse(!is.na(e2_tab$p) && e2_tab$p < .05,
                     "SUPPORTED in this sample", "not supported in this sample")))
}
```

```{r phase3_e2_sensitivity}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 3.3 — E2 SPECIFICATION CHECKS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reruns E2 under two alternative specifications and
# stacks all three side by side, so the preregistered result can be read next to
# the choices that produced it.
#
# PRODUCES: `e2_sens_tab`; output/tables/E2_solidarity_steiger.csv.
# ===========================================================================

# Sensitivity 1: put Solidarity_1 back into the Durkheimian composite.
# This is the specification a reader who disagrees with the Section 5.3 item
# judgement would run. Since Solidarity_1 ("Removing criminals from society
# helps society cleanse itself") reads as exclusionary, including it should move
# the Durkheimian composite TOWARD the hostile one, shrinking the very
# difference E2 predicts. If E2 holds in the preregistered specification and
# weakens here, that pattern is itself evidence the item is exclusionary; if the
# two specifications agree, the item choice was not load-bearing. Either way the
# reader gets to judge, which is why both are printed rather than one.
e2_sens <- steiger_overlap(d, "punitiveness", "exclusion", "solidarity_all",
                           alternative = "greater")

# Sensitivity 2: E2 inside the retributivist group only (Section 5.3 asks for
# every contrast under each measure; H11 reruns the whole-sample tests there).
# The ranking definition is used because it is the primary categorical grouping.
# Restricting to it costs statistical power, so a weaker result here is expected
# on n alone and should not be read as a failure to replicate.
d_retrib <- d[!is.na(d$retributivist) & d$retributivist == 1, , drop = FALSE]
e2_retrib <- steiger_overlap(d_retrib, "punitiveness", "exclusion",
                             "solidarity_durk", alternative = "greater")

# cbind() prefixes each table with a `spec` column naming its specification, so
# the stacked table can never be read without knowing which row is which. The
# preregistered row is listed first and labelled as such.
e2_sens_tab <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null), list(
  if (!is.null(e2))        cbind(spec = "preregistered (S2+S3, whole sample)", e2$table),
  if (!is.null(e2_sens))   cbind(spec = "sensitivity: Solidarity_1 included",  e2_sens$table),
  if (!is.null(e2_retrib)) cbind(spec = "retributivists only (ranking)",       e2_retrib$table)
)))
show_table(e2_sens_tab, caption = "E2 — specification checks")
if (!is.null(e2_sens_tab))
  readr::write_csv(e2_sens_tab, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "E2_solidarity_steiger.csv"))
cat("\nWrote output/tables/E2_solidarity_steiger.csv\n")
```

# PHASE 4: FACTOR STRUCTURE OF THE CORRELATES (EFA + SCREE)

Section 6.6 asks for "the factor structure of the correlates" as an exploratory
extension of H3, which summarizes the intercorrelations by "the share that are
positive and by the first eigenvalue and scree of an exploratory factor
analysis." The correlate set is the one named in H1.

```{r phase4_correlate_matrix}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 4.1 — THE CORRELATE INTERCORRELATION MATRIX
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: assembles the twelve H1 correlates, reports the share of
# positive intercorrelations, the mean and range, and the eigenvalues.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: the exploratory extension of H3 that Section 6.6 asks for. H3
# itself (Section 6.3) summarizes the correlate intercorrelations "by the share
# that are positive and by the first eigenvalue and scree of an exploratory
# factor analysis, to see whether one punitiveness dimension runs through them."
# This is that question asked one level deeper -- not just how big the first
# eigenvalue is, but what the factors look like once extracted.
#
# NO HYPOTHESIS TEST LIVES HERE. This is a descriptive decomposition with no
# null, which is one of the concrete reasons a single BH sweep across this
# document would be meaningless: there is nothing in this phase for a
# false-discovery rate to be a rate OF.
#
# OBJECTS CREATED: correlates, efa_data, cm, ev -- all used by 4.2 and 4.3.
# PRODUCES: output/tables/EFA_correlate_intercorrelations.csv.
# ===========================================================================

# The H1 correlate set, in the order Sections 5.5 - 5.9 introduce them: the
# Kantian limits, the emotions, exclusion, the harshness measures, revenge, and
# the crime concerns. Every one is scored so that HIGHER = more punitive, which
# is what makes "share positive" a meaningful summary rather than an artifact of
# keying: a mixed-key set would show negative cells that mean agreement.
correlates <- intersect(
  c("dueprocess", "uncertain", "hatred", "anger", "exclusion", "degradation",
    "suffering", "prisonviol", "harsh", "revenge", "crimerates", "fear"),
  names(d))

# LISTWISE for the factor analysis: psych::fa() needs one covariance matrix from
# one set of rows, and a pairwise matrix can come out non-positive-definite,
# producing Heywood cases and impossible communalities.
efa_data <- d[, correlates, drop = FALSE]
efa_data <- efa_data[stats::complete.cases(efa_data), , drop = FALSE]
cat(sprintf("EFA on %d correlates, complete cases N = %d\n",
            length(correlates), nrow(efa_data)))

# PAIRWISE for the descriptive matrix, which is the opposite choice and a
# deliberate one: the printed r's and the share-positive count should use every
# available pair rather than being restricted to the listwise subset, so each
# cell is the best estimate of that particular correlation.
cm <- stats::cor(d[, correlates], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
# upper.tri() takes each pair once: 12 correlates give 12*11/2 = 66 unique
# off-diagonal cells, and using the full matrix would double-count every one.
offdiag <- cm[upper.tri(cm)]
cat(sprintf("\nShare of positive intercorrelations: %s (%d of %d)\n",
            pct(mean(offdiag > 0)), sum(offdiag > 0), length(offdiag)))
cat(sprintf("Mean intercorrelation: r = %.3f (range %.3f to %.3f)\n",
            mean(offdiag), min(offdiag), max(offdiag)))

# Eigenvalues of the CORRELATION matrix, so they sum to the number of variables
# (12) and each one reads as "how many variables' worth of variance". A large
# first eigenvalue relative to the rest is what "one punitiveness dimension runs
# through them" would look like.
ev <- eigen(cm)$values
cat(sprintf("First eigenvalue: %.2f of %d (%s of the variance)\n",
            ev[1], length(ev), pct(ev[1] / sum(ev))))
# The Kaiser criterion: a component with an eigenvalue above 1 accounts for more
# variance than a single standardized variable does. It is reported because it
# is conventional and because it anchors the dashed line on the scree plot, but
# it is known to over-retain, which is why the number of factors actually
# extracted in 4.3 comes from parallel analysis instead.
cat(sprintf("Eigenvalues > 1: %d\n", sum(ev > 1)))

# The zero matrix passed as p_matrix stars every off-diagonal cell. That is
# intentional: this table displays the SIGN PATTERN that H3 summarizes, and its
# 66 cells are not 66 tests. Passing real p-values would invite exactly the
# cell-by-cell reading Section 6.6 rules out for this document.
show_table(format_cor_table(cm, matrix(0, nrow(cm), ncol(cm),
                                       dimnames = dimnames(cm)), 2),
           caption = "Intercorrelations among the H1 correlates")
readr::write_csv(
  data.frame(variable = rownames(cm), round(cm, 3), check.names = FALSE),
  file.path(OUT_TABLES, "EFA_correlate_intercorrelations.csv"))
```

```{r phase4_scree, fig.height=5}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 4.2 — SCREE PLOT
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The scree Section 6.3 names as part of the H3 summary. Read it for the ELBOW:
# a single steep drop from the first eigenvalue into a flat tail is the shape a
# one-dimensional punitiveness construct produces, while two comparable
# eigenvalues before the flattening indicate the correlates split.
#
# PRODUCES: output/figures/EFA_scree_correlates.png.
# ===========================================================================
scree_df <- data.frame(factor = seq_along(ev), eigenvalue = ev)
p_scree <- ggplot2::ggplot(scree_df, ggplot2::aes(x = factor, y = eigenvalue)) +
  # The Kaiser line at 1.0: a component below it explains less than one
  # standardized variable's worth of variance.
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  # One break per component: the x axis is a count, so ggplot's default
  # continuous breaks would print meaningless half-components.
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = scree_df$factor) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Scree plot of the punitiveness correlates",
    subtitle = sprintf("First eigenvalue = %.2f (%s of variance); dashed line at 1.0",
                       ev[1], pct(ev[1] / sum(ev))),
    x = "Component", y = "Eigenvalue") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
print(p_scree)
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "EFA_scree_correlates.png"),
                p_scree, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)
cat("Saved: output/figures/EFA_scree_correlates.png\n")
```

```{r phase4_efa}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 4.3 — EXPLORATORY FACTOR ANALYSIS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: chooses a number of factors by parallel analysis,
# extracts at that solution, and prints the loadings twice -- once in full, once
# with small loadings suppressed.
#
# PRODUCES: `efa_fit`, `load_df`, `disp`;
#           output/tables/EFA_correlate_loadings.csv.
# ===========================================================================

# Parallel analysis for the number of factors, then an EFA at that solution.
# WHY PARALLEL ANALYSIS: it compares each observed eigenvalue against the
# eigenvalues of random data with the same n and the same number of variables,
# and retains a factor only when it beats what chance alone produces at this
# sample size. That is a stricter and better-calibrated rule than the Kaiser
# criterion reported in 4.1, which over-retains as the variable count grows.
# fa = "fa" runs the comparison on the common-factor solution rather than on
# principal components, matching the psych::fa() extraction used below.
# n.iter = 50 random datasets is enough for a stable count at N in the hundreds.
# The max(1, min(., 4)) clamp is a guardrail, not a finding: it keeps a
# degenerate result from requesting zero factors (which errors) or more factors
# than twelve correlates can support with interpretable loadings. A solution
# that hits the ceiling of 4 should be read as "at least four", and the
# eigenvalues in 4.1 are the check on that.
n_fac <- tryCatch({
  pa <- psych::fa.parallel(efa_data, fa = "fa", n.iter = 50,
                           plot = FALSE, show.legend = FALSE)
  max(1, min(pa$nfact, 4))
}, error = function(e) { cat("Parallel analysis failed:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"); 2 })

cat(sprintf("Factors retained: %d\n\n", n_fac))

# ROTATION. Oblimin is OBLIQUE: it lets the extracted factors correlate, which
# is the theoretically right assumption here, since H3 is precisely the claim
# that one punitiveness dimension runs through the correlates. Forcing the
# factors orthogonal with varimax would assume that answer away -- it would
# guarantee uncorrelated factors and then invite the reader to conclude the
# correlates are independent. The varimax branch exists only so the document
# knits without GPArotation; when HAS_GPA is FALSE the loadings change and the
# Phi matrix below disappears, so the rotation actually used is printed in the
# table caption rather than assumed.
rot <- if (HAS_GPA) "oblimin" else "varimax"
# fm = "ml" is maximum likelihood, which yields interpretable fit statistics and
# is the natural companion to a factor model. It can fail to converge on a
# near-singular matrix, so the fallback drops to psych::fa()'s default minres
# (ordinary least squares), which is far more forgiving; the message names which
# one ran so nobody compares an ML solution against an OLS one unknowingly.
efa_fit <- tryCatch(
  psych::fa(efa_data, nfactors = n_fac, rotate = rot, fm = "ml"),
  error = function(e) {
    cat("ML extraction failed, falling back to minres:", conditionMessage(e), "\n")
    tryCatch(psych::fa(efa_data, nfactors = n_fac, rotate = rot),
             error = function(e2) NULL)
  })

load_df <- NULL
disp    <- NULL
if (!is.null(efa_fit)) {
  # unclass() strips psych's "loadings" class, whose print method hides small
  # values by default -- exactly the suppression this chunk wants to control
  # explicitly rather than inherit.
  load_mat <- unclass(efa_fit$loadings)
  # h2 is the COMMUNALITY: the share of each correlate's variance the retained
  # factors account for. A correlate with a low h2 is one the factor solution
  # essentially fails to explain, which matters as much as a high loading does.
  load_df  <- data.frame(variable = rownames(load_mat),
                         round(load_mat, 3),
                         h2 = round(efa_fit$communality, 3),
                         # check.names = FALSE keeps psych's factor column names
                         # (ML1, ML2, ...) intact.
                         check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  # Suppressed view: loadings below |.30| blanked, for readability.
  # .30 is the conventional threshold for a loading worth interpreting: it is
  # roughly where a variable shares 9% of its variance with a factor. The
  # ABSOLUTE value is what matters, so a strong negative loading survives.
  # BOTH views are printed rather than only the suppressed one, because
  # suppression hides cross-loadings, and a correlate loading .28 on two factors
  # is a substantively different finding from one loading .28 on neither.
  # The same .30 threshold marks a near-zero loading in the H6 factor model
  # (Section 6.4), where poor fit OR a loading below it counts as failure to
  # cohere; that test lives in 01_main_analysis.Rmd, not here.
  disp <- load_df
  # Everything except the label and the communality column is a factor column.
  fac_cols <- setdiff(names(disp), c("variable", "h2"))
  # sprintf() converts the survivors to character, so each factor column becomes
  # character as a whole and the blanks sit in it without coercion warnings.
  for (cc in fac_cols)
    disp[[cc]] <- ifelse(abs(disp[[cc]]) < .30, "", sprintf("%.2f", disp[[cc]]))
}

show_table(load_df,
           caption = sprintf("EFA loadings (%d factors, %s rotation, ML)", n_fac, rot))
show_table(disp, caption = "EFA loadings with |lambda| < .30 suppressed")

if (is.null(efa_fit)) {
  cat("EFA could not be estimated on this sample.\n")
} else {
  # Row 2 of Vaccounted is "Proportion Var", the share of total variance each
  # factor explains. (Row 1 is the raw SS loadings, row 3 the cumulative share.)
  cat(sprintf("Proportion of variance explained: %s\n",
              paste(sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * efa_fit$Vaccounted[2, ]),
                    collapse = ", ")))
  # Phi is the factor intercorrelation matrix and EXISTS ONLY under an oblique
  # rotation -- varimax constrains it to the identity, so psych returns NULL and
  # the guard skips it. This is the most directly H3-relevant number in the
  # phase: strongly correlated factors say the correlates are facets of one
  # punitiveness dimension, while near-zero Phi says they are genuinely separate
  # even though an oblique rotation was free to let them correlate.
  if (n_fac > 1 && !is.null(efa_fit$Phi)) {
    cat("\nFactor intercorrelations (Phi):\n")
    print(round(efa_fit$Phi, 3))
  }
  readr::write_csv(load_df, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "EFA_correlate_loadings.csv"))
  cat("\nWrote output/tables/EFA_correlate_loadings.csv\n")
}
```

# PHASE 5: CHANGE FROM THE FIRST TO THE SECOND SENTENCE

The second sentence is set after the forward-looking reasons for punishment are
removed (the defendant is permanently disabled and no longer a danger, and
procedural rules remove any prospect of general deterrence). Whatever punishment
survives that removal reflects desert (Section 5.11).

Two indices are examined: the raw change (`Sentence2 - Sentence1`), and the
pre-registered **sentencing ratio** (`Sentence2 / Sentence1` for participants
whose first sentence was above zero). Section 5.11 prefers the ratio because the
raw drop is bounded by the first sentence and piles up at zero, and it asks for
the **regression-adjusted** version — the second sentence residualized on the
first — as a robustness check. Section 5.11 also asks that results be confirmed
**within each vignette**.

Throughout this phase, punitiveness is the 8-item self-report scale: the sentence
is on the other side of every test here, so the full index would double-count it.

## 5.1 Descriptives of the change

```{r phase5_change_desc}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 5.1 — DESCRIPTIVES OF THE SENTENCE CHANGE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: describes both change indices, tests the drop with a
# paired t-test, reports the two boundary behaviours (no reduction at all, and
# reduction to zero), and breaks the whole picture down by vignette.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: the first-to-second sentence analysis Section 6.6 asks for,
# specified in Section 5.11.
# OBJECTS CREATED: `sentence_delta`, used by 5.2 and saved in Phase 9.
# ===========================================================================

# The raw change. NEGATIVE means the participant reduced the sentence, which is
# the expected direction once the forward-looking reasons are removed.
# Section 5.11 prefers the ratio to this index "because the raw drop is bounded
# by the first sentence and is expected to pile up at zero" -- someone who set
# 5 years cannot drop by more than 5, so the raw change confounds the size of
# the reduction with the size of the original sentence. Both are reported; the
# ratio is the one carried into the analyses below.
d$sentence_delta <- d$Sentence2 - d$Sentence1

# The median is shown alongside the mean throughout, because both indices are
# expected to be skewed with mass at a boundary and the mean alone would
# misdescribe the typical participant.
sent_desc <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Sentence1 (years)", "Sentence2 (years)",
              "change (S2 - S1)", "ratio (S2 / S1)"),
  n = c(sum(!is.na(d$Sentence1)), sum(!is.na(d$Sentence2)),
        sum(!is.na(d$sentence_delta)), sum(!is.na(d$sentence_ratio))),
  M = c(mean(d$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE), mean(d$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE),
        mean(d$sentence_delta, na.rm = TRUE), mean(d$sentence_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)),
  SD = c(stats::sd(d$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE), stats::sd(d$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE),
         stats::sd(d$sentence_delta, na.rm = TRUE), stats::sd(d$sentence_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)),
  Median = c(stats::median(d$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE),
             stats::median(d$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE),
             stats::median(d$sentence_delta, na.rm = TRUE),
             stats::median(d$sentence_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
show_table(sent_desc, caption = "First and second sentence, and the change between them")

# PAIRED, not two-sample: both sentences come from the same participant about
# the same case, so the pairing removes between-participant differences in
# baseline punitiveness and tests only the within-person change. An unpaired
# test here would be answering a different and much less interesting question.
# Two-sided: this is a descriptive check that the manipulation moved sentences
# at all, not one of the directional predictions Section 6.8 tests one-sided.
tt_sent <- stats::t.test(d$Sentence2, d$Sentence1, paired = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("\nPaired test of the drop: t(%.0f) = %.2f, p %s, mean change = %.2f years\n",
            tt_sent$parameter, tt_sent$statistic, format_p(tt_sent$p.value),
            unname(tt_sent$estimate)))
# The two boundary behaviours, reported because they are the substantive
# extremes rather than nuisance cases. A ratio of 1 or above means the
# participant kept (or raised) the whole sentence after being told the defendant
# is permanently disabled and no longer deterrable -- the purest expression of a
# desert motive the design offers. A ratio of 0 means punishment collapsed once
# the forward-looking reasons were withdrawn, the purely consequentialist
# response. The size of these two groups is the headline of this phase, and it
# also explains why the median split on the ratio needs balanced_split().
cat(sprintf("Did NOT reduce at all (ratio >= 1): %s\n",
            pct(mean(d$sentence_ratio >= 1, na.rm = TRUE))))
cat(sprintf("Reduced to zero (ratio = 0): %s\n",
            pct(mean(d$sentence_ratio == 0, na.rm = TRUE))))

# Section 5.11 asks that results be confirmed WITHIN each vignette, because the
# three cases differ in severity. This table sets up that check descriptively;
# 5.4 runs the correlations within vignette.
by_vig <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(stats::na.omit(d$Vignette))), function(v) {
  s <- d[!is.na(d$Vignette) & d$Vignette == v, ]
  data.frame(Vignette = v, n = nrow(s),
             M_S1 = mean(s$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE),
             M_S2 = mean(s$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE),
             M_change = mean(s$sentence_delta, na.rm = TRUE),
             Median_ratio = stats::median(s$sentence_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
show_table(by_vig, caption = "Sentence change by vignette")
```

```{r phase5_change_figure, fig.height=5}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 5.2 — DISTRIBUTION OF THE SENTENCING RATIO BY VIGNETTE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A histogram rather than a summary statistic, because the SHAPE is the finding.
# Section 5.11 predicts a pile-up, and a mean or median cannot show whether the
# ratio is unimodal or splits into a group that cut deeply and a group that did
# not cut at all. Faceting by vignette also makes the Section 5.11 consistency
# check visible: the ratio is a proportion and therefore comparable across
# vignettes, so the three panels should have similar shapes even though the
# underlying sentences differ in severity.
#
# PRODUCES: output/figures/sentence_ratio_by_vignette.png.
# ===========================================================================
plot_df <- d[!is.na(d$sentence_ratio), c("Vignette", "sentence_ratio"), drop = FALSE]
if (nrow(plot_df)) {
  # sort(unique(...)) so the labels attach to the factor levels in the same
  # numeric order factor() creates them; a mismatch here would silently relabel
  # one vignette as another.
  plot_df$Vignette <- factor(plot_df$Vignette,
                             labels = paste("Vignette", sort(unique(plot_df$Vignette))))
  p_ratio <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = sentence_ratio)) +
    # 25 bins is fine enough to resolve the spike at exactly 1.0 without
    # shattering the body of the distribution into noise.
    ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
    # Free-scaled facets are NOT used: the three panels share axes so their
    # shapes can be compared directly, which is the whole point of the check.
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ Vignette) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = "Share of the first sentence retained in the second",
      subtitle = "Higher = smaller reduction once the forward-looking reasons are removed",
      x = "Sentence2 / Sentence1", y = "Participants") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  print(p_ratio)
  ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "sentence_ratio_by_vignette.png"),
                  p_ratio, width = 10, height = 5, dpi = 150)
  cat("Saved: output/figures/sentence_ratio_by_vignette.png\n")
}
```

## 5.2 The change as a function of retributivism

```{r phase5_change_by_retributivism}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 5.3 — THE CHANGE AS A FUNCTION OF RETRIBUTIVISM
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: treats both change indices as OUTCOMES and asks whether
# more retributive participants reduce less. Grouped contrasts first, then the
# continuous regression, then the ratio's correlation with punitiveness.
#
# PRODUCES: `chg_tab`, `chg_cont`; chg_tab is written to
#           output/tables/sentence_change_contrasts.csv in 5.4.
#
# `directions = NULL` on all three contrasts, so every test is TWO-SIDED.
# Section 6.6 lists the sentence change among the report-only analyses and names
# no direction for it, and Section 6.8 reserves one-sided tests for predictions
# that name a direction. E1 and E2 earn one-sided tests; this does not.
# ===========================================================================
change_vars <- c("sentence_delta", "sentence_ratio")

# The sentencing ratio is NOT used to group participants here: it is built from
# the same sentences these outcomes describe (Section 5.3, the H14 restriction).
# grp_ratio would put sentence_ratio on both sides at once and guarantee a large
# effect that means nothing. The same logic bars grp_sem from Phase 5 in
# principle; it is absent here simply because these outcomes are the sentence.
# Three groupings remain: the ranking and the two cuts of the relative subscale.
chg_rank <- run_contrasts(d, change_vars, "grp_rank", NULL,
                          label = "ranking (retribution 1st)")
chg_rel  <- run_contrasts(d, change_vars, "grp_rel", NULL,
                          label = "relative subscale (median split)")
chg_tert <- run_contrasts(d, change_vars, "grp_tert", NULL,
                          label = "relative subscale (top vs bottom third)")

chg_tab <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null), list(chg_rank, chg_rel, chg_tert)))
# `grouping` leads the displayed columns because three definitions are stacked
# here; without it the six rows would be unreadable.
show_table(pick_cols(chg_tab, c("grouping", "variable", "n_low", "n_high", "M_low", "M_high",
                       "t", "p_two_sided", "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
           caption = "Sentence change and ratio by retributivist group")

# Continuous: the change indices on the relative retribution subscale.
# The no-split version required by Section 6.5, using the primary continuous
# measure. Only retribution_rel is used as a predictor -- sentence_ratio would
# be predicting itself, and the semantic measure is a stand-in.
chg_cont <- do.call(rbind, lapply(change_vars, function(v) {
  # Subset before scale(), so the standardization is computed on exactly the
  # rows the model fits and beta reads as the correlation.
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(d[[v]], d$retribution_rel)
  if (sum(ok) < 10) return(NULL)
  fit <- stats::lm(scale(d[[v]][ok]) ~ scale(d$retribution_rel[ok]))
  s <- summary(fit)$coefficients; ci <- stats::confint(fit)
  data.frame(outcome = v, predictor = "retribution_rel", n = sum(ok),
             beta = s[2, 1], t = s[2, 3], p = s[2, 4],
             ci_lo = ci[2, 1], ci_hi = ci[2, 2], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
show_table(chg_cont,
           caption = "Sentence change on the continuous relative retribution subscale")

# And the ratio's relation to the sentence-free punitiveness scale.
# HAZARD: `punitiveness`, never `punitiveness_full`. Sections 5.3 and 5.11 both
# state the rule -- "wherever the sentencing ratio appears together with
# punitiveness, whether as a grouping variable, a predictor, an interaction
# term, or a correlate, we use the self-report punitiveness scale, which does
# not contain the sentence". punitiveness_full embeds Sentence1_z, and
# sentence_ratio is Sentence2/Sentence1, so the full index would put the first
# sentence on both sides and inflate this correlation by construction.
r_ratio_punit <- get_cor_ci("sentence_ratio", "punitiveness", d)
cat(sprintf("\nsentencing ratio x punitiveness (8-item, sentence-free): r = %.3f [%.3f, %.3f], p %s, n = %d\n",
            r_ratio_punit["r"], r_ratio_punit["ci_lower"], r_ratio_punit["ci_upper"],
            format_p(r_ratio_punit["p"]), r_ratio_punit["n"]))
```

## 5.3 Regression-adjusted robustness: the second sentence residualized on the first

```{r phase5_residualized}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 5.4 — REGRESSION-ADJUSTED ROBUSTNESS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: residualizes the second sentence on the first, then
# repeats the group contrasts and correlations on the residual.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: the robustness check Sections 5.3 and 5.11 both name -- "we also
# report the regression-adjusted version (the second sentence residualized on
# the first) as a robustness check."
#
# WHY IT IS THE RIGHT ROBUSTNESS CHECK FOR THE RATIO: the ratio's denominator is
# the first sentence, so any measurement error in Sentence1 enters the index
# twice, and its distribution is bounded and lumpy. The residual from
# Sentence2 ~ Sentence1 asks the same substantive question -- how much
# punishment survives once the forward-looking reasons are gone, holding the
# first sentence constant -- with a linear adjustment instead of a division.
# Agreement between the ratio and the residual means the finding does not depend
# on that functional form.
#
# PRODUCES: sentence2_resid, sentence2_resid_vig, res_grp, res_cor;
#           output/tables/sentence_residualized_correlations.csv and
#           output/tables/sentence_change_contrasts.csv.
# ===========================================================================

# Model A: Sentence2 ~ Sentence1.  Model B adds vignette fixed effects, since
# the three vignettes differ in severity (Section 5.11).
# Both are reported: Model A answers "given how severely this person sentenced
# at first, how much did they keep", while Model B additionally removes the
# vignette mean, so its residual compares a participant only against others who
# read the SAME case. That is the linear counterpart of the within-vignette
# z-scoring applied to the first sentence.
resid_ok <- stats::complete.cases(d$Sentence1, d$Sentence2)
fitA <- fitB <- NULL
res_grp <- res_cor <- NULL

# 20 complete pairs is a floor, not a power calculation: below it a two-predictor
# residual is not worth forming, and the chunk reports that instead of printing
# an unstable model.
if (sum(resid_ok) >= 20) {
  # na.action = na.exclude, NOT the default na.omit. This is what makes the
  # residual vector line up with `d` row for row: na.omit would return a shorter
  # vector with the incomplete rows dropped, and assigning it to a column of `d`
  # would either error or, worse, recycle and attach every residual to the wrong
  # participant. na.exclude pads the gaps with NA and preserves the length.
  fitA <- stats::lm(Sentence2 ~ Sentence1, data = d, na.action = stats::na.exclude)
  d$sentence2_resid <- as.numeric(stats::residuals(fitA))

  # factor(Vignette) rather than the bare numeric column: the vignette codes
  # 1/2/3 are labels, not a quantity, and leaving them numeric would fit a
  # single linear slope across three unrelated cases.
  fitB <- stats::lm(Sentence2 ~ Sentence1 + factor(Vignette), data = d,
                    na.action = stats::na.exclude)
  d$sentence2_resid_vig <- as.numeric(stats::residuals(fitB))

  resid_vars <- c("sentence2_resid", "sentence2_resid_vig")

  # The same three groupings as 5.3, and for the same reason the ratio is absent
  # from them: it is built from the sentences these residuals are built from.
  # Two-sided throughout (directions = NULL), matching 5.3.
  res_grp <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null), list(
    run_contrasts(d, resid_vars, "grp_rank", NULL, label = "ranking (retribution 1st)"),
    run_contrasts(d, resid_vars, "grp_rel",  NULL, label = "relative subscale (median split)"),
    run_contrasts(d, resid_vars, "grp_tert", NULL, label = "relative subscale (top vs bottom third)")
  )))

  # Correlates chosen to span the theoretical range: the retributivism measure
  # itself, punitiveness, revenge, just deserts, and the hostile-aggression
  # cluster. If the residual really indexes a desert motive, it should track
  # just_deserts and retribution_rel at least as closely as it tracks revenge.
  res_cor <- do.call(rbind, lapply(resid_vars, function(v) {
    # `punitiveness` here is again the sentence-free 8-item scale. The residual
    # is a linear function of Sentence1 and Sentence2, so punitiveness_full
    # would share Sentence1_z with it directly.
    do.call(rbind, lapply(c("retribution_rel", "punitiveness", "revenge",
                            "just_deserts", "hostile_agg"), function(p) {
      cc <- get_cor_ci(v, p, d)
      data.frame(residual = v, correlate = p, r = cc["r"],
                 ci_lo = cc["ci_lower"], ci_hi = cc["ci_upper"],
                 p = cc["p"], n = cc["n"], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    }))
  }))
  # lapply over a named vector leaves get_cor_ci()'s element names ("r", "p")
  # as row names on the stacked frame; clearing them keeps the printed table
  # from carrying a meaningless gutter.
  rownames(res_cor) <- NULL
}

# show_table() is called at the TOP LEVEL, with the NULL check inlined as an
# argument rather than wrapping the call in an if/else. knitr only prints the
# value of a top-level expression, so a show_table() buried inside a branch
# would compute its kable and silently discard it.
show_table(if (is.null(fitA)) NULL else broom::tidy(fitA),
           caption = "Model A: Sentence2 ~ Sentence1")
show_table(if (is.null(fitB)) NULL else broom::tidy(fitB),
           caption = "Model B: Sentence2 ~ Sentence1 + vignette")
show_table(pick_cols(res_grp, c("grouping", "variable", "n_low", "n_high",
                                "M_low", "M_high", "t", "p_two_sided",
                                "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
           caption = "Residualized second sentence by retributivist group")
show_table(res_cor,
           caption = "Residualized second sentence: correlations (punitiveness is the sentence-free 8-item scale)")

if (is.null(fitA)) {
  cat("Too few complete Sentence1/Sentence2 pairs for the residualized model.\n")
} else {
  # R-squared here is a diagnostic, not a result: it says how much of the second
  # sentence the first one explains, and therefore how much variance is LEFT in
  # the residual for the contrasts above to work with. A very high R-squared
  # would mean the residual is nearly all noise; the gap between Model A and
  # Model B is the share vignette severity contributes.
  cat(sprintf("Model A: R-squared = %.3f, n = %d\n",
              summary(fitA)$r.squared, stats::nobs(fitA)))
  cat(sprintf("Model B: R-squared = %.3f, n = %d\n",
              summary(fitB)$r.squared, stats::nobs(fitB)))
  readr::write_csv(res_cor, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "sentence_residualized_correlations.csv"))
  cat("Wrote output/tables/sentence_residualized_correlations.csv\n")
}

if (!is.null(chg_tab))
  readr::write_csv(chg_tab, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "sentence_change_contrasts.csv"))
cat("Wrote output/tables/sentence_change_contrasts.csv\n")
```

## 5.4 Within-vignette consistency

```{r phase5_within_vignette}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 5.5 — WITHIN-VIGNETTE CONSISTENCY
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 5.11: "Because the ratio is a proportion it is comparable across
# vignettes, and we confirm that results hold within each vignette." This is
# that confirmation.
#
# WHAT TO READ FOR: consistency of SIGN and rough magnitude across the three
# panels, not significance in each. Each vignette holds roughly 315 people, so a
# correlation that clears alpha in the pooled sample can easily fail to in a
# third of it; three same-signed coefficients of similar size is the result this
# check is looking for, and one reversed sign is the warning.
#
# Both correlates appear: the primary continuous retributivism measure, and
# punitiveness in its sentence-free 8-item form for the reason given in 5.3.
# ===========================================================================
within_vig <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(stats::na.omit(d$Vignette))), function(v) {
  # One vignette's rows at a time, so both correlations are estimated entirely
  # within that case and vignette severity cannot contribute to either.
  s <- d[!is.na(d$Vignette) & d$Vignette == v, , drop = FALSE]
  cc1 <- get_cor_ci("sentence_ratio", "retribution_rel", s)
  cc2 <- get_cor_ci("sentence_ratio", "punitiveness",    s)
  data.frame(Vignette = v, n = nrow(s),
             r_ratio_relretrib = cc1["r"], p_relretrib = cc1["p"],
             r_ratio_punitiveness = cc2["r"], p_punitiveness = cc2["p"],
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
rownames(within_vig) <- NULL
show_table(within_vig,
           caption = "Sentencing ratio within each vignette (Section 5.11 consistency check)")
```

# PHASE 6: POLITICAL ORIENTATION AND PROSECUTION–DEFENSE LEANING AS MODERATORS

Section 5.13 records a single liberal–conservative item (`lib/conserv`, 1 =
strongly liberal to 7 = strongly conservative) and two prosecution–defense items
(`leanPros_1`, `leanPros_2`; 1 = prosecutor, 2 = defense attorney, 3 = about the
same). Section 6.6 asks for both as **moderators**.

The leaning items are recoded to a signed score so that higher means siding with
the prosecution: prosecutor = +1, about the same = 0, defense = -1, averaged
across the two items.

```{r phase6_moderator_vars}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 6.1 — BUILD THE MODERATOR VARIABLES
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: derives the two moderators Section 6.6 asks for and
# prints their descriptives plus the raw response distributions.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: Section 5.13 (the measures) as read by Section 6.6 (use them as
# moderators). OBJECTS CREATED: `libcons`, `pros_lean`.
# ===========================================================================

# The single liberal-conservative item, 1 = strongly liberal to 7 = strongly
# conservative (Section 5.13). Only the two endpoints carry anchor text in the
# instrument; the five interior points are unlabelled, which is why the Values
# export is the only usable one -- the Labels export writes bare numbers there.
# The Qualtrics tag contains a slash, so it needs [[ ]] access; copying it to
# `libcons` lets every model below use ordinary formula syntax.
if ("lib/conserv" %in% names(d)) d$libcons <- as.numeric(d[["lib/conserv"]])
# Create the column as all-NA if the item is absent, so the models downstream
# fail their complete-cases guard cleanly instead of erroring on a missing name.
if (!"libcons" %in% names(d)) d$libcons <- NA_real_

# The two prosecution-defense items export as 1 = prosecutor, 2 = defense
# attorney, 3 = about the same (Qualtrics recodes the raw choice ids 3/4/6 onto
# 1/2/3). That coding is NOMINAL, not ordinal: averaging it raw would place
# "about the same" at the top of the scale rather than between the two sides.
# Recoding to a signed score fixes that -- prosecutor = +1, about the same = 0,
# defense = -1 -- so that higher means siding with the prosecution and the
# midpoint sits where the neutral answer belongs.
recode_lean <- function(x) dplyr::case_when(x == 1 ~ 1, x == 3 ~ 0, x == 2 ~ -1,
                                            TRUE ~ NA_real_)
if (all(c("leanPros_1", "leanPros_2") %in% names(d))) {
  # leanPros_1 asks who the participant identifies with at a real trial;
  # leanPros_2 asks which role they would rather serve. Averaging the two gives
  # a five-point score (-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1) that credits a participant who
  # leans one way on one item and is neutral on the other.
  d$pros_lean <- rowMeans(cbind(recode_lean(d$leanPros_1),
                                recode_lean(d$leanPros_2)), na.rm = TRUE)
  # rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) over two NAs returns NaN, not NA. Left alone, NaN
  # would pass an is.na() test but print as NaN in tables and propagate oddly
  # through mean-centring, so it is normalized to NA here.
  d$pros_lean[is.nan(d$pros_lean)] <- NA_real_
} else {
  d$pros_lean <- NA_real_
}

mod_desc <- data.frame(
  moderator = c("libcons (1 = liberal, 7 = conservative)",
                "pros_lean (-1 = defense, +1 = prosecution)"),
  n  = c(sum(!is.na(d$libcons)),  sum(!is.na(d$pros_lean))),
  M  = c(mean(d$libcons, na.rm = TRUE),  mean(d$pros_lean, na.rm = TRUE)),
  SD = c(stats::sd(d$libcons, na.rm = TRUE), stats::sd(d$pros_lean, na.rm = TRUE)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
show_table(mod_desc, caption = "Moderator descriptives")

if (all(c("leanPros_1", "leanPros_2") %in% names(d))) {
  cat("\nleanPros_1 (trial identification): 1 = prosecutor, 2 = defense, 3 = same\n")
  print(table(d$leanPros_1, useNA = "ifany"))
  cat("\nleanPros_2 (which role would you serve): 1 = prosecutor, 2 = defense, 3 = same\n")
  print(table(d$leanPros_2, useNA = "ifany"))
}
```

```{r phase6_moderator_correlations}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 6.2 — MODERATORS: ZERO-ORDER CORRELATIONS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The main effects, reported before any interaction. An interaction term is
# hard to interpret without knowing how the moderator relates to the outcome on
# its own, and a moderator with no zero-order relation to anything is a
# different situation from one that correlates strongly with everything.
#
# Twelve correlations here, two moderators x six variables, all UNADJUSTED.
# Section 6.6 does not declare them a family, and they are reported as
# descriptive context rather than as tests. Every one carries its CI and n.
# ===========================================================================
mod_cors <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("libcons", "pros_lean"), function(m) {
  # Sentence1_z rather than raw Sentence1: the vignettes differ in severity, so
  # the within-vignette standardized score is the only version comparable across
  # the pooled sample (Section 5.11).
  # `punitiveness` is the sentence-free 8-item scale, which keeps this table
  # readable next to sentence_ratio and Sentence1_z in the same column: no two
  # rows here share a component.
  do.call(rbind, lapply(intersect(c("punitiveness", "retribution_rel",
                                    "sentence_ratio", "hostile_agg",
                                    "Sentence1_z", "revenge"), names(d)),
                        function(v) {
    cc <- get_cor_ci(m, v, d)
    data.frame(moderator = m, variable = v, r = cc["r"],
               ci_lo = cc["ci_lower"], ci_hi = cc["ci_upper"],
               p = cc["p"], n = cc["n"], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}))
rownames(mod_cors) <- NULL
mod_cors$stars <- sig_stars(mod_cors$p)
show_table(mod_cors, caption = "Moderators: zero-order correlations")
```

```{r phase6_moderation_models}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 6.3 — MODERATION MODELS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: fits eight outcome ~ predictor * moderator models and
# extracts only the interaction term from each.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: Section 6.6's request for political orientation and the
# prosecution-defense leaning "as moderators", using the Section 5.13 measures.
#
# EIGHT INTERACTIONS, NO CORRECTION ACROSS THEM. This is the largest single set
# of tests in the document and the most tempting place to apply BH, so the
# reasoning is worth stating: Section 6.6 places these analyses outside both
# preregistered families, and the eight models were never declared as a family
# of their own. Correcting them here would mean inventing a family after seeing
# the data, and the adjusted p it produced would be a researcher degree of
# freedom rather than a control. They are read as descriptive, alongside the
# interaction coefficient and its standard error.
#
# PRODUCES: `mod_results`; output/tables/moderator_interactions.csv.
# ===========================================================================

# Mean-centred predictors so the interaction term is interpretable.
# Centring does NOT change the interaction coefficient or its p-value; what it
# changes is the MAIN effects, which in a product model are conditional on the
# other predictor being zero. Uncentred, the "effect of retributivism" would be
# its effect at libcons = 0, a value off the 1-7 scale entirely. Centred, each
# main effect is the effect at the sample mean of the other, which is a value
# that exists. Centring also cuts the collinearity between a predictor and its
# own product term, keeping the standard errors readable.
ctr <- function(x) x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
d$retrib_rel_c  <- ctr(d$retribution_rel)
d$ratio_c       <- ctr(d$sentence_ratio)
d$libcons_c     <- ctr(d$libcons)
d$pros_lean_c   <- ctr(d$pros_lean)

# The specification grid, declared explicitly rather than generated by crossing
# every predictor with every outcome. Writing it out is what makes the
# punitiveness/ratio restriction below visible and auditable: an automatic
# expand.grid() would happily produce the forbidden pairings.
mod_specs <- list(
  list(y = "punitiveness", x = "retrib_rel_c", m = "libcons_c"),
  list(y = "punitiveness", x = "retrib_rel_c", m = "pros_lean_c"),
  list(y = "hostile_agg",  x = "retrib_rel_c", m = "libcons_c"),
  list(y = "hostile_agg",  x = "retrib_rel_c", m = "pros_lean_c"),
  list(y = "Sentence1_z",  x = "retrib_rel_c", m = "libcons_c"),
  list(y = "Sentence1_z",  x = "retrib_rel_c", m = "pros_lean_c"),
  # The sentencing ratio is paired ONLY with the sentence-free punitiveness
  # scale, per Sections 5.3 and 5.11.
  # HAZARD: there is deliberately no ratio_c x Sentence1_z model in this grid.
  # The ratio is Sentence2/Sentence1 and Sentence1_z is the standardized first
  # sentence, so such a model would regress the sentence on itself. Swapping
  # `punitiveness` for punitiveness_full in the two rows below would smuggle in
  # the same problem, since the full index embeds Sentence1_z.
  list(y = "punitiveness", x = "ratio_c", m = "libcons_c"),
  list(y = "punitiveness", x = "ratio_c", m = "pros_lean_c")
)

mod_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mod_specs, function(s) {
  if (!all(c(s$y, s$x, s$m) %in% names(d))) return(NULL)
  # LISTWISE on the three model variables. Fitting on a common subset means the
  # main effects and the interaction all describe the same participants, and it
  # is what makes `n` in the output table meaningful.
  sub <- d[stats::complete.cases(d[[s$y]], d[[s$x]], d[[s$m]]), , drop = FALSE]
  # 30 complete cases is a floor for a four-parameter model, not a power
  # threshold: below it the interaction's standard error is not worth printing.
  # The models that actually run here have hundreds of cases.
  if (nrow(sub) < 30) return(NULL)
  # `y ~ x * m` expands to y ~ x + m + x:m, so both main effects are in the
  # model. That matters: an interaction fitted without its constituent main
  # effects is not a moderation test at all.
  f   <- stats::as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ %s * %s", s$y, s$x, s$m))
  fit <- stats::lm(f, data = sub)
  tid <- broom::tidy(fit)
  # The product term is the only one whose name contains a colon; that is what
  # identifies it without depending on row position.
  int <- tid[grepl(":", tid$term), , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(int)) return(NULL)
  # Only the interaction is carried out. The main effects are already covered by
  # the zero-order correlations in 6.2 and the contrasts in 6.4, and the
  # moderation question is entirely about this one coefficient. R2 for the whole
  # model is kept as context for how much the three terms explain together.
  # Two-sided p: Section 6.6 asks for these as moderators without predicting a
  # direction for any of them, so Section 6.8 leaves them two-sided.
  data.frame(outcome = s$y, predictor = s$x, moderator = s$m, n = nrow(sub),
             R2 = summary(fit)$r.squared,
             b_interaction = int$estimate[1], se = int$std.error[1],
             t = int$statistic[1], p = int$p.value[1],
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))

if (!is.null(mod_results)) mod_results$stars <- sig_stars(mod_results$p)

show_table(mod_results,
           caption = "Moderation: interaction terms (retributivism x moderator)")

if (is.null(mod_results)) {
  cat("No moderation model had enough complete cases.\n")
} else {
  readr::write_csv(mod_results, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "moderator_interactions.csv"))
  cat("Wrote output/tables/moderator_interactions.csv\n")
}
```

```{r phase6_moderator_groups}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 6.4 — MODERATORS BY RETRIBUTIVIST GROUP
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# How the moderators themselves differ by retributivist group (descriptive; the
# confirmatory version of the prosecution-defense contrast is H18, which lives
# in 01_main_analysis.Rmd).
#
# This table answers the prior question the moderation models raise: whether the
# moderators are themselves confounded with retributivism. If retributivists are
# markedly more conservative, then a null interaction in 6.3 is not evidence
# that ideology is irrelevant -- it may simply have little independent variance
# left once retributivism is in the model. Two-sided throughout, and reported as
# description rather than as a test, since H18 owns the confirmatory version.
#
# grp_ratio IS included here, unlike in Phase 5: libcons and pros_lean are
# demographic items collected after the vignette but built from no part of the
# sentence, so the Section 5.3 circularity restriction does not reach them.
# ===========================================================================
mod_grp <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null), list(
  run_contrasts(d, c("libcons", "pros_lean"), "grp_rank", NULL,
                label = "ranking (retribution 1st)"),
  run_contrasts(d, c("libcons", "pros_lean"), "grp_rel", NULL,
                label = "relative subscale (median split)"),
  run_contrasts(d, c("libcons", "pros_lean"), "grp_ratio", NULL,
                label = "sentencing ratio (median split)")
)))
show_table(pick_cols(mod_grp, c("grouping", "variable", "M_low", "M_high", "t",
                       "p_two_sided", "d", "d_lo", "d_hi")),
           caption = "Moderators by retributivist group (descriptive)")
```

# PHASE 7: AGREEMENT AMONG THE FOUR RETRIBUTIVIST DEFINITIONS

Section 5.3 identifies retributivists with four measures and requires that "we
report their pairwise agreement and the overlap among the groups they define":

  1. **Ranking** — ranks "criminals deserve to be punished" first (primary categorical).
  2. **Relative retribution subscale** — retribution minus the mean of the other
     three goals (primary continuous).
  3. **Sentencing ratio** — `Sentence2 / Sentence1` for first sentences above zero.
  4. **Semantic measure** — retributive facets from the open-ended responses
     (exploratory; see Section 1.4 above for its current status).

```{r phase7_measure_status}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 7.1 — STATUS OF THE FOUR DEFINITIONS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# An inventory printed before any agreement statistic, so every coefficient
# below can be read against the n that produced it and against the standing of
# the measure. The `status` column carries SEMANTIC_STATUS verbatim, which is
# how a word-list stand-in is prevented from being read as the validated
# ensemble score it is not.
# ===========================================================================
measure_status <- data.frame(
  measure = c("1. ranking (categorical)", "2. relative subscale (continuous)",
              "3. sentencing ratio (behavioral)", "4. semantic (exploratory)"),
  variable = c("retributivist", "retribution_rel", "sentence_ratio",
               "semantic_retributivism"),
  n_available = c(sum(!is.na(d$retributivist)), sum(!is.na(d$retribution_rel)),
                  sum(!is.na(d$sentence_ratio)), sum(!is.na(d$semantic_retributivism))),
  status = c("available", "available", "available", SEMANTIC_STATUS),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
show_table(measure_status, caption = "Status of the four retributivist definitions")
```

## 7.1 Pairwise agreement (continuous)

```{r phase7_pairwise_continuous}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 7.2 — PAIRWISE AGREEMENT (CONTINUOUS)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# IMPLEMENTS: Section 5.3's requirement that, since the four definitions are
# treated as convergent, "we report their pairwise agreement and the overlap
# among the groups they define."
#
# WHY THIS MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING BOOKKEEPING: Section 5.3 expects every
# single measure to be imperfect -- demand characteristics push self-reports
# toward the utilitarian goals, people punish on desert while reporting
# utilitarian aims, and introspective access to punitive motive is limited. If
# the four definitions agreed strongly, one would do; if they agree only
# modestly, then the E1 tables that run every contrast four times are not
# redundancy but the actual evidence, and a result that appears under one
# definition alone should be read as being about that measure.
#
# `retributivist` is 0/1, so any correlation involving it is a POINT-BISERIAL
# coefficient. Pearson's formula computes it correctly, and the table caption
# says so; the constraint to notice is that its maximum attainable magnitude is
# limited by how unbalanced the 0/1 split is, so a modest r against a continuous
# measure understates agreement rather than overstating it.
# ===========================================================================
meas_cont <- intersect(c("retributivist", "retribution_rel", "sentence_ratio",
                         "semantic_retributivism"), names(d))
# combn(..., 2) gives each unordered pair once: four measures produce six pairs,
# and simplify = FALSE keeps them as a list of character vectors to lapply over.
pairs_cont <- utils::combn(meas_cont, 2, simplify = FALSE)

agree_cont <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pairs_cont, function(pp) {
  cc <- get_cor_ci(pp[1], pp[2], d)
  data.frame(measure_1 = pp[1], measure_2 = pp[2],
             r = cc["r"], ci_lo = cc["ci_lower"], ci_hi = cc["ci_upper"],
             p = cc["p"], n = cc["n"], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
rownames(agree_cont) <- NULL
agree_cont$stars <- sig_stars(agree_cont$p)
show_table(agree_cont,
```
