```{r phase7_pairwise_continuous}
           caption = "Pairwise agreement among the retributivist measures (r; the ranking enters as 0/1, so its coefficients are point-biserial)")
```

## 7.2 Overlap among the groups they define

```{r phase7_overlap}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 7.3 — OVERLAP AMONG THE GROUPS THE DEFINITIONS CREATE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The second half of the Section 5.3 requirement: not how the four measures
# correlate, but how much the GROUPS they define actually overlap. Four agreement
# statistics are reported per pair because they answer four different questions
# and can disagree sharply:
#
#   pct_agreement  the share of participants both definitions classify the same
#                  way. Inflated whenever both groups are small, since agreeing
#                  that most people are NOT retributivists is easy.
#   jaccard        both-high / either-high. Ignores the agreed-low cell, so it
#                  measures overlap among the people the study is about.
#   kappa          agreement corrected for what chance would produce given the
#                  observed marginals. The honest headline number.
#   phi            the correlation between the two 0/1 vectors, comparable to
#                  the continuous r's in 7.2.
#
# A pair with high percent agreement and low kappa is the diagnostic pattern:
# it means the two definitions agree mostly by both calling people non-
# retributivist, not by picking out the same retributivists.
# ===========================================================================
grp_defs <- list(
  ranking  = d$retributivist,
  relative = d$retrib_medsplit,
  ratio    = d$ratio_medsplit,
  semantic = d$sem_medsplit
)
# Drop any definition with no data at all -- typically the semantic placeholder.
# Doing it here rather than inside the loop keeps combn() from generating pairs
# that could never be computed, and keeps the convergence count in 7.4 honest
# about how many definitions were actually available.
grp_defs <- grp_defs[vapply(grp_defs, function(x) sum(!is.na(x)) > 0, logical(1))]

pairs_bin <- if (length(grp_defs) >= 2)
  utils::combn(names(grp_defs), 2, simplify = FALSE) else list()

overlap_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pairs_bin, function(pp) {
  a <- grp_defs[[pp[1]]]; b <- grp_defs[[pp[2]]]
  ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
  if (sum(ok) < 10) return(NULL)
  a <- a[ok]; b <- b[ok]
  # factor(., 0:1) forces both levels to exist so the table is always 2x2 even
  # when a cell is empty; a collapsed table would break the statistics below.
  tab <- table(factor(a, 0:1), factor(b, 0:1))

  # cohen.kappa() takes the two classifications as columns and treats them as
  # two raters judging the same participants -- which is exactly the frame
  # Section 5.3 sets up, with the four measures as competing "raters" of who
  # counts as a retributivist. $kappa is the unweighted coefficient, which is
  # the right one for an unordered binary judgement.
  kap <- tryCatch(psych::cohen.kappa(cbind(a, b))$kappa,
                  error = function(e) NA_real_)
  # For two binary variables the Pearson correlation IS the phi coefficient, so
  # cor() is not an approximation here.
  phi <- tryCatch(stats::cor(a, b), error = function(e) NA_real_)
  both <- sum(a == 1 & b == 1)
  either <- sum(a == 1 | b == 1)

  data.frame(
    definition_1 = pp[1], definition_2 = pp[2], n = sum(ok),
    # The marginals are printed alongside the agreement statistics because kappa
    # and Jaccard cannot be interpreted without them: two definitions that
    # nominate very different numbers of retributivists are capped in how much
    # they can ever agree.
    n_high_1 = sum(a == 1), n_high_2 = sum(b == 1),
    n_both_high = both,
    pct_agreement = mean(a == b),
    # Guard against 0/0 when neither definition nominates anyone.
    jaccard = ifelse(either > 0, both / either, NA_real_),
    kappa = kap, phi = phi,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))

if (!is.null(overlap_tab)) rownames(overlap_tab) <- NULL

show_table(overlap_tab,
           caption = "Group overlap: percent agreement, Jaccard, Cohen's kappa, phi")

if (is.null(overlap_tab))
  cat("Not enough overlapping data to compute group agreement.\n")

# The raw 2x2 tables behind every statistic above. Printed in full so a reader
# can recompute any of the four coefficients by hand, and so the cell that
# drives a surprising kappa is visible rather than inferred.
cat("\nCross-tabulations:\n")
for (pp in pairs_bin) {
  a <- grp_defs[[pp[1]]]; b <- grp_defs[[pp[2]]]
  ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
  if (sum(ok) < 10) next
  cat(sprintf("\n%s (rows) x %s (cols), 0 = low / 1 = high:\n", pp[1], pp[2]))
  print(table(factor(a[ok], 0:1), factor(b[ok], 0:1)))
}
```

```{r phase7_convergence_note}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 7.4 — CONVERGENCE COUNT AND AGREEMENT EXPORT
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The pairwise tables in 7.3 cannot say how many participants ALL the
# definitions agree about. This one can: it counts, for each participant, how
# many definitions place them in the high group, and tabulates that count.
#
# READ THE TAILS. Participants scoring high on every available definition are
# the unambiguous retributivists, and the size of that group is what a reader
# should have in mind whenever the four E1 tables in Phase 2 disagree. A count
# distribution concentrated at 1 or 2 says the definitions are picking out
# largely different people, which is Section 5.3's stated expectation and the
# reason it demands every contrast under each measure.
#
# PRODUCES: output/tables/retributivist_measure_agreement.csv and
#           output/tables/retributivist_group_overlap.csv.
# ===========================================================================

# How many participants land in the high group on 1, 2, 3, or all 4 definitions.
gm <- as.data.frame(grp_defs)
conv <- NULL
if (ncol(gm) >= 2) {
  # Every column is 0/1, so the row sum IS the number of definitions calling
  # this participant high. na.rm = TRUE means a missing definition counts as a
  # non-vote rather than voiding the row, which is why n_meas is recorded too.
  gm$n_high <- rowSums(gm, na.rm = TRUE)
  # How many definitions were actually available for this participant. Without
  # it, someone scored by two definitions and high on both is indistinguishable
  # from someone scored by four and high on two.
  gm$n_meas <- rowSums(!is.na(gm[, names(grp_defs), drop = FALSE]))
  conv <- as.data.frame(table(gm$n_high))
  names(conv) <- c("n_definitions_high", "n_participants")
  conv$pct <- conv$n_participants / sum(conv$n_participants)
}
show_table(conv,
           caption = sprintf("Convergence: how many of the %d available definitions place a participant in the high group",
                             length(grp_defs)))

# One long export combining both kinds of agreement. `kind` distinguishes them,
# because a Pearson r and a Cohen's kappa share a column here and must never be
# averaged or compared as though they were the same quantity. The kappa rows
# carry p = NA deliberately: cohen.kappa()'s significance test is not extracted,
# since these coefficients are reported as descriptive convergence rather than
# as tests of a null of no agreement.
agree_out <- do.call(rbind, Filter(Negate(is.null), list(
  if (!is.null(agree_cont))
    data.frame(kind = "continuous r", agree_cont[, c("measure_1", "measure_2",
                                                     "r", "p", "n")],
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  if (!is.null(overlap_tab))
    data.frame(kind = "group overlap kappa",
               measure_1 = overlap_tab$definition_1,
               measure_2 = overlap_tab$definition_2,
               r = overlap_tab$kappa, p = NA_real_, n = overlap_tab$n,
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
)))
if (!is.null(agree_out)) {
  readr::write_csv(agree_out, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "retributivist_measure_agreement.csv"))
  cat("\nWrote output/tables/retributivist_measure_agreement.csv\n")
}
if (!is.null(overlap_tab))
  readr::write_csv(overlap_tab, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "retributivist_group_overlap.csv"))
cat("Wrote output/tables/retributivist_group_overlap.csv\n")
```

# PHASE 8: RESPONSE-QUALITY REPORT (COMPLETION TIME AND LONG STRINGS)

Section 6.2: "We also examine completion time and long strings of identical
answers and report them, but **neither on its own removes a participant from the
confirmatory analyses**." This phase is therefore a **diagnostic report only**.
No participant is excluded on the basis of anything below, and the confirmatory
document (01) does not read these flags.

## 8.1 Completion time

```{r phase8_duration}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 8.1 — COMPLETION TIME
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: describes completion time and computes three speeding /
# lingering flags.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: Section 6.2, which asks that completion time be examined and
# reported but is explicit that "neither on its own removes a participant from
# the confirmatory analyses." Nothing computed here feeds an exclusion. The
# exclusions were applied in Phase 1.1 and are the Section 6.2 grounds that act on
# the export:
# unfinished, and the two attention checks.
#
# OBJECTS CREATED: duration_s, flag_fast_half, flag_fast_third, flag_slow.
# ===========================================================================

# Three spellings, because the column name depends on how the file was read:
# readr preserves "Duration (in seconds)" verbatim, base R's read.csv mangles it
# to "Duration..in.seconds.", and a file already processed by 01 may carry the
# tidy name. intersect() takes whichever exists.
dur_col <- intersect(c("Duration (in seconds)", "Duration..in.seconds.",
                       "duration_s"), names(d))

dur_desc <- NULL
med_dur  <- NA_real_

if (!length(dur_col)) {
  d$duration_s <- NA_real_
} else {
  d$duration_s <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d[[dur_col[1]]]))
  dur     <- d$duration_s
  # The MEDIAN, not the mean, anchors every threshold below. Completion time is
  # heavily right-skewed -- a handful of participants leave the tab open for
  # hours -- and a mean-based cutoff would be dragged upward by them, flagging
  # ordinary respondents as too fast.
  med_dur <- stats::median(dur, na.rm = TRUE)

  dur_desc <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("n", "minimum", "1st quartile", "median", "mean",
                  "3rd quartile", "maximum"),
    seconds = c(sum(!is.na(dur)), min(dur, na.rm = TRUE),
                stats::quantile(dur, .25, na.rm = TRUE), med_dur,
                mean(dur, na.rm = TRUE),
                stats::quantile(dur, .75, na.rm = TRUE), max(dur, na.rm = TRUE)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  dur_desc$minutes <- dur_desc$seconds / 60
  # Row 1 of the table is the COUNT of participants, not a duration, so its
  # "minutes" cell would be a meaningless n/60. Blanked rather than printed.
  dur_desc$minutes[1] <- NA

  # Two conventional speeding heuristics, reported side by side.
  # Both are the standard fractions of the median used in survey screening:
  # under half the median is the lenient version, under a third the strict one.
  # Reporting both makes the reader's sensitivity to the choice visible instead
  # of hiding it behind one number, which matters precisely because no
  # participant is removed on either basis.
  d$flag_fast_half  <- as.integer(dur < 0.50 * med_dur)
  d$flag_fast_third <- as.integer(dur < (1/3) * med_dur)
  # The mirror image: more than three times the median. This is NOT a
  # carelessness indicator in the way speeding is -- it usually marks an
  # interrupted session -- and it is reported for completeness rather than as
  # evidence of low-quality responding.
  d$flag_slow       <- as.integer(dur > 3 * med_dur)
}

show_table(dur_desc, caption = "Completion time")

if (!length(dur_col)) {
  cat("No completion-time column in the input; this section is a placeholder.\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf("Median completion time: %.0f s (%.1f min)\n", med_dur, med_dur / 60))
  cat(sprintf("Faster than 1/2 the median (< %.0f s): %d participants (%s)\n",
              0.5 * med_dur, sum(d$flag_fast_half, na.rm = TRUE),
              pct(mean(d$flag_fast_half, na.rm = TRUE))))
  cat(sprintf("Faster than 1/3 the median (< %.0f s): %d participants (%s)\n",
              (1/3) * med_dur, sum(d$flag_fast_third, na.rm = TRUE),
              pct(mean(d$flag_fast_third, na.rm = TRUE))))
  cat(sprintf("Slower than 3x the median (> %.0f s): %d participants (%s)\n",
              3 * med_dur, sum(d$flag_slow, na.rm = TRUE),
              pct(mean(d$flag_slow, na.rm = TRUE))))
}
```

```{r phase8_duration_figure, fig.height=5}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 8.2 — COMPLETION-TIME DISTRIBUTION
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The histogram behind the thresholds in 8.1. Its job is to show whether the
# fast tail is a distinct cluster of speeders or simply the lower end of one
# continuous distribution -- the flags cannot distinguish those two, and the
# subtitle repeats that no one is excluded on this basis.
#
# PRODUCES: output/figures/response_quality_duration.png.
# ===========================================================================
if (sum(!is.na(d$duration_s))) {
  p_dur <- ggplot2::ggplot(d[!is.na(d$duration_s), ],
                           # Plotted in MINUTES for legibility; every threshold
                           # in 8.1 is computed in seconds.
                           ggplot2::aes(x = duration_s / 60)) +
    ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
    # The median line, the anchor all three flags are defined against.
    ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = stats::median(d$duration_s, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
                        linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
    ggplot2::labs(title = "Completion time",
                  subtitle = "Dashed line at the median. Reported only — no one is excluded on this basis.",
                  x = "Minutes", y = "Participants") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  print(p_dur)
  ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "response_quality_duration.png"),
                  p_dur, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)
  cat("Saved: output/figures/response_quality_duration.png\n")
}
```

## 8.2 Long strings of identical answers

```{r phase8_longstring}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 8.3 — LONG STRINGS OF IDENTICAL ANSWERS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: computes each participant's longest run of identical
# consecutive answers across the attitude battery, and the share of their
# answers at their own modal value.
#
# IMPLEMENTS: the second half of the Section 6.2 diagnostic. Again REPORT ONLY.
#
# WHAT A LONG STRING IS AND IS NOT: it is the classic straight-lining indicator,
# but this battery contains reverse-keyed items scattered throughout, so a
# genuinely consistent respondent should NOT produce a long run -- agreeing with
# both a punitiveness item and its reversed neighbour requires different
# numbers. That is what makes the measure informative here. It is still not
# proof of inattention: a participant who scores 7 on every hostility item in a
# block may simply hold that view strongly.
#
# OBJECTS CREATED: longstring, modal_response, flag_longstring.
# ===========================================================================

# The attitude battery, in questionnaire order, so that a "long string" means a
# run of identical answers as the participant actually saw them. Only the 1-7
# agree/disagree style items are used; sliders and categorical items are not.
# ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING. rle() below finds runs of ADJACENT identical values, so
# this vector must match the presentation order of Sections 5.2 through 5.12; a
# resorted list would report runs the participant never actually produced.
# Excluded by design: the sentence sliders and CRT sliders (a continuous 0-50
# response is not a scale point), the categorical demographics, and both
# attention checks (whose sparse coding would break the run logic and which have
# already done their work in the exclusion funnel).
ls_items <- intersect(c(
  paste0("Retribution_", 1:7), paste0("Deterrence_", 1:3),
  paste0("Incapacitation_", 1:2), paste0("Rehabilitation_", 1:2),
  paste0("Solidarity_", 1:3),
  "punishmore_1", "punishmore_2", "parsimony_1", "parsimony_2",
  "threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2", "LWOP", "deathpenalty",
  paste0("revenge_", 1:4), "proportionality", "severity_1", "severity_2",
  paste0("exclusion_", 1:3), paste0("essential_", 1:4),
  paste0("Society_", 1:3), paste0("choice_", 1:2),
  paste0("dueprocess_", 1:3), paste0("uncertain_", 1:4),
  paste0("rates_", 1:2), paste0("fear_", 1:3),
  paste0("hate_", 1:3), paste0("anger_", 1:2),
  paste0("degrad_", 1:3), paste0("suffer_", 1:2), paste0("prisonvi_", 1:2),
  paste0("harsh_", 1:3), paste0("rwa_", 1:5), paste0("sdo_", 1:8),
  paste0("vprone_", 1:4), paste0("Raceresent_", 1:4)), names(d))

cat(sprintf("Long-string computed over %d attitude items.\n", length(ls_items)))

#' Longest run of identical consecutive values in one participant's row.
#' Arguments: x, one row of the item matrix. Returns: integer run length, or NA.
#' rle() encodes the vector as runs and reports each run's length; the maximum
#' of those lengths is the long-string index. Note that rle() treats each NA as
#' breaking a run, so a skipped item shortens rather than extends the count --
#' the conservative direction for a flag nobody is excluded on.
max_run <- function(x) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  if (all(is.na(x))) return(NA_integer_)
  r <- rle(x)
  as.integer(max(r$lengths, na.rm = TRUE))
}
#' Share of a participant's answers sitting at their own most-frequent value.
#' Arguments: x, one row. Returns: proportion in 0-1, or NA for an empty row.
#' This is the POSITION-FREE companion to max_run(): it catches a participant
#' who answered 4 to three quarters of the battery but never in a long
#' consecutive block, which rle() would miss entirely.
modal_share <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (!length(x)) return(NA_real_)
  max(table(x)) / length(x)
}

ls_desc <- NULL

# Fewer than 10 items makes a run length uninformative -- with a short battery
# almost any answer pattern produces a "long" relative run.
if (length(ls_items) >= 10) {
  # as.matrix() so apply() walks rows of a uniform numeric matrix. Applying over
  # a data frame would coerce each row through a list and be far slower.
  mat <- as.matrix(d[, ls_items, drop = FALSE])
  d$longstring     <- apply(mat, 1, max_run)
  d$modal_response <- apply(mat, 1, modal_share)

  ls_desc <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("n", "minimum", "median", "mean", "90th percentile",
                  "95th percentile", "maximum"),
    longest_run = c(sum(!is.na(d$longstring)),
                    min(d$longstring, na.rm = TRUE),
                    stats::median(d$longstring, na.rm = TRUE),
                    mean(d$longstring, na.rm = TRUE),
                    stats::quantile(d$longstring, .90, na.rm = TRUE),
                    stats::quantile(d$longstring, .95, na.rm = TRUE),
                    max(d$longstring, na.rm = TRUE)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # 10 consecutive identical answers is the conventional straight-lining
  # threshold, and it is a demanding one in THIS battery: reaching it means
  # giving the same number to ten adjacent items that include reverse-keyed
  # ones. The 15-run count printed below shows how sensitive the tally is to
  # moving the line, which is the honest way to report a threshold that
  # determines nothing.
  d$flag_longstring <- as.integer(d$longstring >= 10)
}

show_table(ls_desc, caption = "Longest run of identical consecutive answers")

if (length(ls_items) >= 10) {
  cat(sprintf("Runs of 10 or more identical answers: %d participants (%s)\n",
              sum(d$flag_longstring, na.rm = TRUE),
              pct(mean(d$flag_longstring, na.rm = TRUE))))
  cat(sprintf("Runs of 15 or more: %d participants (%s)\n",
              sum(d$longstring >= 15, na.rm = TRUE),
              pct(mean(d$longstring >= 15, na.rm = TRUE))))
  cat(sprintf("Median share of responses at the participant's modal value: %s\n",
              pct(stats::median(d$modal_response, na.rm = TRUE))))
  cat("\nDistribution of the longest run:\n")
  print(table(d$longstring, useNA = "ifany"))
} else {
  d$longstring <- NA_integer_
  d$flag_longstring <- NA_integer_
  cat("Too few attitude items present to compute long strings.\n")
}
```

```{r phase8_quality_summary}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 8.4 — RESPONSE-QUALITY FLAG SUMMARY
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Collects the four flags into one table and builds `flag_any`, the union used
# by the sensitivity comparison in 8.5.
#
# The flags OVERLAP by construction: flag_fast_third is a strict subset of
# flag_fast_half, so the four counts must not be added together. flag_any is
# computed as a union rather than a sum for exactly that reason.
#
# PRODUCES: output/tables/response_quality_flags.csv.
# ===========================================================================
flag_cols <- intersect(c("flag_fast_half", "flag_fast_third", "flag_slow",
                         "flag_longstring"), names(d))
qual <- NULL

if (length(flag_cols)) {
  qual <- data.frame(
    flag = flag_cols,
    n_flagged = sapply(flag_cols, function(f) sum(d[[f]], na.rm = TRUE)),
    # mean() of a 0/1 column is the proportion flagged; na.rm keeps a
    # participant with a missing duration from voiding the whole figure.
    pct_flagged = sapply(flag_cols, function(f) mean(d[[f]], na.rm = TRUE)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  # sapply() over a named vector puts the flag names on the rows as well as in
  # the `flag` column; clearing them avoids printing the same labels twice.
  rownames(qual) <- NULL
  # "> 0" makes this a UNION: flagged on at least one indicator. A row sum would
  # double-count the nested speeding flags and produce a meaningless total.
  d$flag_any <- as.integer(rowSums(d[, flag_cols, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE) > 0)
}

show_table(qual, caption = "Response-quality flags (report only)")

if (length(flag_cols)) {
  cat(sprintf("Flagged on at least one indicator: %d of %d (%s)\n",
              sum(d$flag_any, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(d),
              pct(mean(d$flag_any, na.rm = TRUE))))
  cat("These participants REMAIN in every analysis (pre-registration 6.2).\n")
  readr::write_csv(qual, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "response_quality_flags.csv"))
  cat("Wrote output/tables/response_quality_flags.csv\n")
} else {
  cat("No response-quality indicator could be computed from this input.\n")
}
```

```{r phase8_quality_sensitivity}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 8.5 — REPORT-ONLY SENSITIVITY
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Report-only sensitivity: does E1 look different with flagged participants set
# aside? This is shown to document the flags' consequences, not to justify
# dropping anyone. Section 6.2 is explicit that neither completion time nor a
# long string removes a participant from the analyses, and the reported result
# everywhere else in this document is the full-sample one.
#
# WHAT THIS BUYS: the column that matters is d_change. If setting the flagged
# participants aside barely moves the effect sizes, then the choice not to
# exclude them costs nothing and the preregistered rule is vindicated on the
# data as well as in principle. If it moved them a lot, that would be worth
# saying out loud -- which is why the comparison is printed rather than
# summarized.
#
# E1 under the RANKING definition is used because it is the primary categorical
# grouping; running all four here would multiply the tables without adding to
# the point, which is about the flags rather than about E1.
# ===========================================================================
cmp <- NULL
n_clean <- NA_integer_

if ("flag_any" %in% names(d) && sum(d$flag_any, na.rm = TRUE) > 0) {
  # is.na(flag_any) is KEPT, not dropped: a participant with no duration
  # recorded was never flagged, and excluding them would confound "flagged" with
  # "missing metadata".
  d_clean <- d[is.na(d$flag_any) | d$flag_any == 0, , drop = FALSE]
  n_clean <- nrow(d_clean)

  # Same outcomes, same directions, same helper as Phase 2.1 -- only the sample
  # differs, which is what makes the two columns comparable.
  e1_sens <- run_contrasts(d_clean, e1_vars, "grp_rank", e1_dir,
                           label = "ranking, flagged set aside")
  if (!is.null(e1_sens) && !is.null(e1_rank)) {
    # merge() by outcome name rather than cbind() by position: if a contrast
    # became non-estimable in the smaller sample, its row simply drops out
    # instead of silently pairing the wrong two effect sizes.
    cmp <- merge(
      pick_cols(e1_rank, c("variable", "d", "p_directional")),
      pick_cols(e1_sens, c("variable", "d", "p_directional")),
      by = "variable", suffixes = c("_full", "_sensitivity"))
    # Signed, so the direction of the shift is visible: positive means setting
    # the flagged participants aside made the effect larger.
    cmp$d_change <- cmp$d_sensitivity - cmp$d_full
  }
}

if (!is.na(n_clean))
  cat(sprintf("Sensitivity sample (flagged set aside): N = %d of %d\n",
              n_clean, nrow(d)))

show_table(cmp,
           caption = "E1 under the ranking definition: full sample vs. flagged set aside")

if (is.na(n_clean))
  cat("No participant was flagged, so no sensitivity comparison is needed.\n")
```

# PHASE 9: SAVE ALL OUTPUT FILES

```{r phase9_save}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 9.1 — SAVE THE DERIVED VARIABLES
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: writes the participant-level variables this document
# created, the reliability log, and (if the fallback ran) the exclusion funnel;
# then lists what is on disk.
#
# WRITES: data/cleaned/retribution_supplementary_vars.csv,
#         output/tables/supplementary_reliability.csv,
#         output/tables/exclusion_funnel_supp.csv (fallback path only).
# ===========================================================================

# The supplementary variables derived in this document, keyed by ResponseId so
# they can be merged back without duplicating the scored file that 01 owns.
# ONLY the columns this document adds are exported -- the composites rebuilt in
# Phase 1.2 are deliberately absent, because 01 owns those and writing a second
# copy here would create two files that could drift apart. intersect() means a
# variable that was never computed (the semantic measure, say) is simply omitted
# rather than exported as a column of NA.
keep <- intersect(c("ResponseId", "Vignette", "retributivist", "retribution_rel",
                    "retrib_medsplit", "retrib_tertile", "sentence_ratio",
                    "ratio_medsplit", "semantic_retributivism", "sem_medsplit",
                    "sentence_delta", "sentence2_resid", "sentence2_resid_vig",
                    "libcons", "pros_lean", "duration_s", "longstring",
                    "modal_response", "flag_fast_half", "flag_fast_third",
                    "flag_slow", "flag_longstring", "flag_any"), names(d))

supp <- d[, keep, drop = FALSE]
readr::write_csv(supp, file.path(OUT_DATA, "retribution_supplementary_vars.csv"))
cat(sprintf("Wrote data/cleaned/retribution_supplementary_vars.csv (%d x %d)\n",
            nrow(supp), ncol(supp)))

# The full reliability log, including the `items` column, so every alpha and
# omega in the appendix can be traced to the exact item list that produced it.
readr::write_csv(alpha_table, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "supplementary_reliability.csv"))
cat("Wrote output/tables/supplementary_reliability.csv\n")

# Written only when the Phase 1.1 fallback ran, i.e. when this document had to
# apply the exclusions itself. On the normal path 01 owns and reports the funnel
# and there is nothing to duplicate.
if (!is.null(exclusion_funnel)) {
  readr::write_csv(exclusion_funnel, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "exclusion_funnel_supp.csv"))
  cat("Wrote output/tables/exclusion_funnel_supp.csv (funnel reproduced locally)\n")
}

cat("\nFiles in output/tables/:\n")
print(list.files(OUT_TABLES))
cat("\nFiles in output/figures/:\n")
print(list.files(OUT_FIGURES))
```

```{r phase9_summary}
# ===========================================================================
# PHASE 9.2 — CLOSING SUMMARY
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A single block a reader can check the knitted document against: which input
# was used, the analysis N, the size of the primary retributivist group, the
# standing of the semantic measure, and the Section 6.6 checklist of everything
# this document was required to deliver.
#
# It closes by restating the multiplicity position, because that is the one
# thing a reader must carry away from every p-value above: no false-discovery
# correction is applied anywhere in this file. Section 6.6 declares two families
# and this document belongs to neither -- the H1 correlation set is corrected in
# 01_main_analysis.Rmd, and E3-E7 are corrected within themselves in
# 02_nlp_integration.Rmd. Everything here is a lead, not a finding.
# ===========================================================================
cat("========================================================================\n")
cat("SUPPLEMENTARY / EXPLORATORY ANALYSES — SUMMARY\n")
cat("========================================================================\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Data source : %s\n", DATA_SOURCE))
cat(sprintf("Analysis N  : %d\n", nrow(d)))
cat(sprintf("Retributivists (ranking): %d (%s)\n",
            sum(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE), pct(mean(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE))))
cat(sprintf("Semantic measure: %s\n\n", SEMANTIC_STATUS))

cat("Delivered in this document (pre-registration 6.6):\n")
cat("  E1  personality + CRT between groups, under all four definitions\n")
cat("  E2  hostile vs Durkheimian solidarity, Steiger's test\n")
cat("      (Solidarity_1 dropped per 5.3; sensitivity with it included)\n")
cat("  --  factor structure of the correlates (EFA + scree)\n")
cat("  --  first-to-second sentence change, incl. residualized robustness\n")
cat("  --  political orientation and prosecution-defense leaning as moderators\n")
cat("  --  agreement and overlap among the four retributivist definitions (5.3)\n")
cat("  --  completion time and long strings, report only (6.2)\n\n")

cat("Not corrected as a confirmatory family (6.6). No FDR adjustment applied.\n")
cat("These are exploratory analyses on the full sample; not a confirmatory family.\n")
```
